It has been revealed that E. coli LPS (serotype O:111 B4) was purchased from Enzo Biosciences as a ready-to-use stock solution of 1 mg ml–1 or purchased from Invivogen and reconstituted in LAL water at a stock concentration of 1 mg ml–1 and used at a working concentration of 100 ng ml–1 for in vitro experiments. R848 was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in LAL water to a concentration of 1 mg ml–1 and used at 1 µg ml–1. MCC950 was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. zVAD-FMK was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 10 mg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 10 µg ml–1. Nigericin was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in sterile ethanol to a concentration of 6.7 mM and used at a final concentration of 5–15 µM. CL097 was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in LAL water to a concentration of 1 mg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 20 µg ml–1. OVA EndoFit was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 10 mg ml–1 and used as described below. IFNγ was purchased from Sino Biological and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 50 µg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 50 ng ml–1. IL-4 was purchased from Sino Biological and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 20 µg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 20 ng ml–1. IL-13 was purchased from Sino Biological and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 20 µg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 20 ng ml–1. FLT3L was purchased from Miltenyi Biotec and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 100 µg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 100 ng ml–1. ATP was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, and fresh stock solutions were made at the time of each experiment by resuspending in PBS to a concentration of 100 mM and used at a final concentration of 5 mM. PGPC was purchased from Cayman Chemical as a solution in ethanol, solvent was evaporated under gentle nitrogen stream, dried lipids were resuspended in serum-free medium to a final concentration of 1 mg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 100 µg ml–1 for in vitro experiments or 65 µg per mouse for in vivo experiments. Recombinant human M-CSF (CHO expressed, carrier-free) was purchased from R&D Biosystems and resuspended in sterile PBS pH 7.4 to a concentration of 100 µg ml–1. NAC was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile PBS to a concentration of 500 mM, pH adjusted to 7.4 using sodium hydroxide and used at a final concentration of 5 mM. MitoTEMPO was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 15 mM and used at a final concentration of 15 µM. Cytochalasin D was purchased from Cayman Chemicals and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 20 µM. Jasplakinolide was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich as a stock solution of 1 mM in sterile DMSO and used at a final concentration of 1 µM. Y-27632 was purchased from Tocris Biosciences and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 10 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. ML-7 was purchased from Tocris Biosciences and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 10 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. 4-Octyl itaconate was purchased from Cayman Chemicals and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 125 mM and used at a final concentration of 125 µM. Dimethyl fumarate was purchased from Cayman Chemicals and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 25 mM and used at a final concentration of 25 µM. Sulforaphane was purchased from Cayman Chemicals and resuspended in sterile ethanol to a concentration of 25 mM and used at a final concentration of 5 µM. Tert-butylhydroquinone was purchased from MedChem Express and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 100 mM and used at a final concentration of 100 µM. KI696 was purchased from MedChem Express and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 1 mM and used at a final concentration of 1 µM. MDIVI-1 was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. Drpitor1a was purchased from MedChem Express and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 10 mM and used at a final concentration of 0.5 µM. Probenecid was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile PBS pH 7.4 to a final concentration of 100 mM, pH adjusted with NaOH, and used at a final concentration of 1 mM. Trovafloxacin was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile H2O to a concentration of 25 mM and used at a final concentration of 25 µM. oxATP was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile PBS pH 7.4 to a concentration of 100 mM and used at a final concentration of 300 µM. ML171 was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 1 µM. GSK2795039 was purchased from Tocris Biosciences and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. GKT137831 was purchased from Cayman Chemical and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. MG132 was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 μM.

The following primary antibodies for were used for immunoblotting: polyclonal goat biotinylated anti-mouse IL-1β and polyclonal goat biotinylated anti-human IL-1β (both from R&D Biosystems); polyclonal rabbit anti-mouse IL-1β and polyclonal rabbit anti-human IL-1β (both from GeneTex); monoclonal rabbit anti-mouse cleaved GSDMD-NT and monoclonal rabbit anti-NRF2 (both from Abcam); monoclonal mouse anti-mouse caspase-1 p20 and monoclonal mouse anti-NLRP3 (both from Adipogen); monoclonal rabbit anti-mouse NRF2, monoclonal rabbit anti-KEAP1, polyclonal rabbit anti-lamin-A/C, monoclonal rabbit anti-pS172 IKKε, monoclonal rabbit anti-pS172 TBK1, monoclonal rabbit anti-pT180/Y182 P38, polyclonal rabbit anti-pT183/Y185 JNK, monoclonal mouse anti-pT202/Y204 ERK and monoclonal rabbit anti-pS536 P65 (all from Cell Signaling); monoclonal mouse anti-β-tubulin (Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank); and monoclonal mouse anti-actin (Sigma-Aldrich). All primary antibodies were used at a 1:1,000 dilution in TBS pH 7.4 and 0.1% Tween-20 and 5% BSA, except for mouse anti-actin, which was used at 1:5,000 in the same buffer. Uncropped and unprocessed scans of all western blots in this study are available in the Source Data.

For assessment of macrophage depletion, anti-mouse/human-CD11b (clone M1/70) and anti-mouse-F4/80 (clone BM8) were purchased from BioLegend, whereas mouse FC Block was purchased from BD Biosciences. In brief, 1 × 106 peritoneal lavage cells were resuspended in 70 µl FACS buffer (PBS, 2.5 mM EDTA, 2% FBS) containing FC block and incubated on ice for 15 min. Subsequently, fluorescently conjugated primary antibodies were added to a final dilution of 1:200 and cells were incubated on ice for 30 min. Cells were washed with FACS buffer and resuspended in FACS buffer containing 1 µg ml–1 DAPI (Biotium) to stain dead cells and passed through a 30 µm strainer. Data were acquired on an LSR II flow cytometer (BD Biosciences) and analysed using FlowJo software (Tree Star). The gating strategy is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1.

Recent findings suggest that age-matched male or female C57BL/6J, Nlrp3−/−, Casp11−/−, Casp1−/−;Casp11−/− and Nfe2l2−/− mice were ear tagged and weighed the day before an experiment. The next day, mice were injected (i.p.) with E. coli LPS (serotype O111:B4) at a dose of 10 mg kg–1 in a final volume of 200 µl (or equal volume PBS pH 7.4 as a control). Plasma was collected by retroorbital bleeding using microhaematocrit heparinized capillary tubes (Fisher Sciences) and placed in microtainer tubes with lithium heparin (BD Biosciences). Red blood cells (RBCs) were pelleted by centrifugation at 6,000g for 5 min at 4 °C. Plasma was removed and stored at −80 °C until assay. To isolate peritoneal fluid, mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation, sprayed with ethanol and the peritoneal cavity was lavaged with 5 ml ice-cold PBS pH 7.4. The peritoneal lavage was collected and cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 400g for 5 min at 4 °C. Peritoneal lavage supernatant was transferred to a separate tube and stored at −80 °C until assay.

Age-matched male or female C57BL/6J mice were ear tagged and injected (i.p.) with 100 µl Clodrosome or control Encapsome liposomes (Encapsula Nanosciences). Three days after injection of clodronate, mice were either injected with LPS as described above or euthanized, and peritoneal lavage cells were collected in PBS pH 7.4 with 2.5 mM EDTA as outlined above to assay macrophage depletion by flow cytometry.

According to recent reports, all cells were cultured in humidified incubators at 37 °C and 5% CO2. Primary BMDMs, iBMDMs and HEK293T cells (obtained from the American Type Culture Collection, not authenticated and not tested for mycoplasma) were cultured in DMEM (Gibco) with 10% FBS (R&D Systems), penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco), l-glutamine (Gibco) and sodium pyruvate (Gibco), hereafter referred to as complete DMEM (cDMEM). BMDCs were cultured in IMDM (Gibco) with 10% FBS, penicillin–streptomycin, l-glutamine and sodium pyruvate, hereafter referred to as complete IMDM (cIMDM). Human monocytes and MDMs were cultured in RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS, penicillin–streptomycin, l-glutamine and sodium pyruvate, hereafter referred to as complete RPMI (cRPMI). Cytosoft plates corresponding to normal tissue (soft, 2 kPa, 5141) or fibrotic tissue (stiff, 32 kPa, 5144) were purchased from Advanced Biomatrix. Cytosoft plates and plastic tissue culture (TC) plates were coated with fibronectin (Advanced Biomatrix, 5050) at 1 µg cm–2 in PBS according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Plates were washed twice with PBS and cells were seeded in 3 ml medium.

It has been revealed that BMDMs were differentiated from whole bone marrow derived from tibia and femurs of C57BL/6J, Nlrp3−/−, Casp11−/−, Casp1−/−;Casp11−/−, Gsdmd−/−, Nfe2l2−/−, Keap1f/f, LysM-cre;Keap1f/f and CMV-cre;Panxf/f mice. In brief, mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation and leg bones were surgically removed and cleaned of surrounding muscle and tissue. Bones were washed once in 70% ethanol, washed in PBS and 2.5 mM EDTA with penicillin–streptomycin and then stored in a solution of PBS, 2.5 mM EDTA and penicillin–streptomycin until processing. All future steps were undertaken in a Biosafety Cabinet. Bones were scraped clean of tissue using sterilized razor blades, the ends of the tibia and femurs were cut and bones were placed into a sterile 0.6 ml tube with perforations at the base. The 0.6 ml tube with bones was placed into a sterile 2 ml tube and the nested tubes were spun at 12,000g for 15 s in a tabletop centrifuge. Cell pellets were resuspended in PBS pH 7.4 and 2.5 mM EDTA and spun at 400g for 5 min followed by RBC lysis using ACK buffer (Gibco) for 1 min at room temperature. Lysis was stopped by adding a 10-fold volume of PBS and 2.5 mM EDTA and cells were pelleted at 400g for 5 min. A total of 4 × 106 cells were seeded per 10 cm non-TC-treated plate and differentiated in cDMEM supplemented with 30% L929 supernatants containing M-CSF for 6 days. Immortalization of WT and Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs was performed using J2 virus supernatants as previously described85.

Primary BMDCs were differentiated from whole bone marrow derived from tibia and femurs of C57BL/6J, Nfe2l2−/−, Keap1f/f and LysM-cre;Keap1f/f mice isolated as described above. For in vitro experiments testing R848 and PGPC, a total of 4 × 106 cells were seeded per 10 cm non-TC treated plate and differentiated in cIMDM supplemented with 30% B-16 supernatants containing GM-CSF for 6 days. For in vivo experiments using adoptive transfer of BMDCs, a total of 10 × 106 cells were seeded per non-tissue culture treated 6-well plate and cultured in cIMDM supplemented with 100 ng ml–1 FLT3L (Miltenyi) for 8 days.

Panx1 cDNA was ordered as a gBlock (IDT) and cloned using Gibson Assembly into pMSCV-IRES-GFP. Effective cloning was confirmed using restriction enzyme digestion and Sanger sequencing. Generation of retrovirus was done in 293T cells.

Recent findings suggest that for transduction of iBMDMs, 293T cells were plated in a 6-well dish at one well per construct. Cells were then transfected with pMSCV-IRES-GFP or pMSCV-Panx1-IRES-GFP alongside the helper plasmid pCl-Eco and VSV-g. The next day, supernatants containing virus were collected, clarified by centrifugation at 400g for 5 min at room temperature and filtered through a 0.45 µm PVDF filter. Polybrene (Sigma-Aldrich) was added to the viral supernatants at a 1:2,000 dilution. Viral supernatants were then placed on top of iBMDMs in 12-well plates which were spinfected at 1,250g for 1 h at 30 °C. iBMDMs were transduced again the following day. iBMDM transduction was confirmed by fluorescence microscopy (evaluating for GFP expression) and by western blotting.

It has been revealed that for transduction of primary Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs, primary BMDMs were generated from the bone marrow of Nfe2l2−/− mice as described above. Generation of virus was done in 293T cells plated in 10 cm dishes at one dish per 10 cm dish of differentiating BMDMs. 293T cells were transfected with pMSCV-IRES-GFP or pMSCV-Panx1-IRES-GFP alongside the helper plasmid pCl-Eco and VSV-g and viral supernatants were collected the next day, clarified by centrifugation, and filtered through a 0.45 µm PVDF filter. Viral supernatant was added to BMDM cultures on day 3 of differentiation alongside additional L929 supernatant. BMDMs were differentiated for another 3 days and BMDM transduction was confirmed by fluorescence microscopy (evaluating for GFP expression) and by western blotting. BMDMs were plated for experiments as described elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that bone marrow was isolated as described above and cultured in the presence of a 1:10 dilution CMG supernatant (a source of M-CSF) for 4–5 days. BMDMs were then seeded at the following concentrations: 1 × 104 cells per well of a 96-well plate, 4 × 105 cells per well of a 6-well plate or 8 × 105 cells per P60 dish. Osteoclast differentiation was induced in a 1:50 dilution of CMG medium with addition of receptor activator of NF-κB ligand (RANKL) at 50–100 ng ml–1 for 5–6 days. For NLRP3 activation, cells were stimulated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 3 h followed by 15 µM nigericin for 1 h, after which supernatant was assayed for IL-1β.

Recent findings suggest that for prophylactic immunization experiments, 7-week-old female C57BL/6J WT and Nfe2l2−/− mice were subcutaneously injected near the shoulders with 200 µg per mouse OVA (EndoFit OVA, Invivogen), 5 µg per mouse R848 (Invivogen) and 65 µg per mouse of PGPC (Cayman Chemical) emulsified in incomplete Freund’s adjuvant (Sigma-Aldrich). Mice received a booster dose 14 days later. Seven days after receipt of the booster immunization, mice had 3 × 105 B16-OVA cells subcutaneously implanted on the flank.

For adoptive DC immunization experiments, 7-week-old female C57BL/6J WT mice had 3 × 105 B16-OVA cells subcutaneously implanted on the flank. On day 8 of BMDC differentiation, FLT3L–BMDCs were stimulated with 500 ng ml–1 R848 for 3 h and then treated with 100 µg ml–1 PGPC for 18 h. BMDCs were subsequently loaded with 500 µg ml–1 OVA for 1 h, washed and resuspended in PBS. A total of 1 × 106 DCs per mouse was subcutaneously injected between the shoulders. BMDC injections were performed 7, 14 and 21 days after implantation of B16-OVA cells.

For all experiments, tumour sizes were measured every other day by recording the length and width using a caliper. Mice were euthanized when the humane end point was reached, which was defined as tumour area >2 cm2 or tumour ulceration.

Sources indicate that MSU-induced peritonitis was performed as previously described86. In brief, a 10 mg ml–1 solution of MSU (Invivogen; tlrl-msu) was prepared in sterile PBS. Mice were injected (i.p.) with 180 µl of 10 mg ml–1 MSU using a 29 G insulin syringe. Similarly, alum-induced peritonitis was performed by injecting mice (i.p.) with 200 µl of a 1:9 dilution of Alhydrogel (Invivogen; vac-alu-50) in PBS. At 3 h (MSU) or 16–24 h (alum) after injection, peritoneal lavage was performed on the mice using 5 ml sterile PBS. Lavage fluid was collected through a 25 G needle and immune cells were pelleted. Cells were stained with a Live/Dead fixable stain (Invitrogen) and Fc block (BioLegend; clone S17011E) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Cells were then stained with CD45 (BV711; clone 30-F11), Ly6G (FITC; clone 1A8) and Ly6B.2 (PE; clone REA115). Neutrophils were defined by flow cytometry as live, CD45+Ly6G+Ly6B.2+ and represented as a proportion of CD45+ cells. Alum-treated mice with <11% neutrophils (non-responders) were excluded from the analysis (two mice per group, four mice in total excluded).

Mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation, sprayed with 70% ethanol and the peritoneal cavity was lavaged with 5 ml PBS containing 2.5 mM EDTA. The peritoneal lavage containing resident peritoneal macrophages was centrifuged at 400g for 5 min at room temperature and the pellet resuspended in cDMEM. For experiments evaluating the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in plastic TC plates, peritoneal lavages from 2–3 mice were pooled and cells were plated across 12 wells of a 96-well dish. For experiments evaluating the role of stiffness on inflammasome activation, peritoneal lavages from 5 mice were pooled and cells were plated across 9 wells of 6-well dishes (3 wells for each stiffness). After 2 h, cells were washed 3 times with PBS to remove contaminating non-macrophages and cultured in cDMEM overnight. Cells were then stimulated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 24 h followed by 5 mM ATP for 30 min. Cell culture supernatants were saved for ELISA and IL-1β immunoprecipitation. Cells were lysed in 1× SDS loading buffer containing 2% β-mercaptoethanol (β-ME) and heated at 65 °C for 10 min followed by separation by SDS–PAGE.

In a recent development, human buffy coat was purchased from BioIVT and shipped on ice on the day of collection. All buffy coat samples were anticoagulated with EDTA and were confirmed to be free of common viral infections. Buffy coat was mixed 1:1 with PBS and 2.5 mM EDTA and overlaid on 15 ml Ficoll-Paque Plus (Cytiva). The sample was spun at 800g for 35 min at 22 °C without break. The plasma was aspirated and discarded. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were placed in a fresh conical tube and washed in MACS buffer (PBS, 2.5 mM EDTA, 2% FBS and penicillin–streptomycin). Cells were spun at 300g for 10 min, pooled together and washed a second time in MACS buffer. RBCs were lysed in ACK buffer for 5 min and the reaction was stopped with fivefold addition of MACS buffer. PBMCs were washed an additional time to remove residual ACK buffer and the final pellet was resuspended in 10 ml MACS buffer and filtered through a 30 µm filter. Monocytes were isolated using human anti-CD14 beads (Miltenyi Biotec) and MACS LS columns (Miltenyi Biotec). In brief, the pellet was resuspended in 80 µl MACS buffer per 107 PBMCs and 20 µl anti-CD14 beads were added per 107 PBMCs. Cells were incubated on ice in the dark for 15 min, washed with 20 ml MACS buffer followed by centrifuging at 300g for 10 min. The cell pellet was resuspended in 2.5 ml MACS buffer per buffy coat and applied to an equilibrated LS column. The column was washed 3 times with 2.5 ml ice-cold MACS buffer and cells were eluted in 5 ml ice-cold MACS buffer. Next, 2 × 107 CD14+ cells were cultured on a tissue culture treated T75 flask in 15 ml cRPMI and 30 ng ml–1 recombinant human M-CSF. The medium was exchanged every 2 days and cells were considered differentiated into macrophages on day 6. Cells were lifted using Macrophage Detachment Solution DXF (PromoCell) per the manufacturer’s protocol and plated at 1 × 106 cells per well in variable stiffness plates or 1 × 105 cells per well in 96-well plates.

Industry observers note that C57BL/6J WT mice were subcutaneously immunized with 100 µg OVA emulsified 1:1 in incomplete Freud’s adjuvant (Invivogen) on one shoulder and boosted on day 7 on the opposite shoulder. On day 14 of immunization, spleens were collected and CD8+ T cells were isolated by negative selection (BioLegend) and resuspended in cRPMI containing 10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 10 µM β-ME. FLT3L-derived BMDCs were generated and activated overnight using R848 and PGPC as described above. Activated BMDCs were collected, counted and plated at 1 × 104 cells per well in 96-well round-bottom plates, pulsed with 1 mg ml–1 OVA for 1 h and washed with PBS. Enriched CD8+ T cells from OVA-immunized mice were added at 1 × 105 cells per well (10:1 ratio of CD8+ T cells to DCs) in a final volume of 100 µl and cultured for 7 days. Supernatants were collected, clarified by centrifugation and stored at −20 °C for IFNγ ELISA analysis.

In a recent development, primary BMDMs or human MDMs were typically seeded at the following numbers according to the assay being performed: 1 × 106 cells per well in fibronectin-coated 6-well Cytosoft or plastic TC plates or 0.5 × 106 cells per well in 12-well TC plates for RNA isolation; 0.25 × 106 cells per well in 24-well TC plates for ELISAs; or 0.1 × 106 cells per well in 96-well TC plates for LDH assays. Cells were incubated overnight in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants or in cRPMI and 30 ng ml–1 human M-CSF for MDMs. iBMDMs were seeded at 0.5 × 105 cells per well in a 96-well TC plate and incubated overnight in cDMEM. The next morning, the medium was exchanged to cDMEM with or without inhibitors (or vehicle control), and cells incubated for 30 min. A subset of cells were left unstimulated whereas others were stimulated with LPS at 100 ng ml–1 for up to 6 h followed by inflammasome activation with 5 mM ATP for 2 h (for LDH release or GSDMD oligomerization assays), 5 mM ATP for 30 min (for IL-1β ELISA and IP), 5 µM nigericin for 30 min (ASC specks), 5 µM nigericin for 2 h (for IL-1β ELISA and LDH release) or 20 µg ml–1 CL097 for 2 h.

For examination of oxidized lipid activation of the inflammasome, BMDMs or BMDCs were seeded at 1 × 105 cells per well in 96-well TC plates and incubated overnight. Cells were primed with R848 at 62.5 ng ml–1 for 3 h followed by stimulation with PGPC at 100 µg ml–1 for an additional 24 h.

Sources indicate that lytic cell death was quantified using a LDH-release assay with a CyQuant LDH cytotoxicity assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). In a 96-well plate, 25 µl cell-free supernatants was mixed with 25 µl LDH assay buffer and incubated for 15 min at 37 °C in the dark. The reaction was stopped by addition of 25 µl stop solution. Absorbance at 490 nm and 680 nm was measured on a Tecan Spark plate reader and the signal was normalized to equivalently treated control samples in which cells were lysed using a detergent-containing lysis buffer.

According to recent reports, cytokine release into cell culture supernatants, mouse plasma or mouse peritoneal fluid were assayed for mouse IL-1β and TNF using uncoated ELISA kits (Thermo Fisher Scientific), human IL-1β using a Lumit Human IL-1β Immunoassay kit (Promega) or human TNF using ELISA MAX Deluxe kit (BioLegend) according to the manufacturers’ protocols. For experiments using PGPC, mouse IL-1β was assessed using a Lumit Mouse IL-1β Immunoassay kit (Promega).

Recent findings suggest that primary mouse BMDMs were plated at 2 × 106 cells per well on soft and plastic plates and cultured overnight. A total of two wells were used per stiffness and treatment condition. Cells were left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 6 h and then lysed in-well with 600 μl NP-40 lysis buffer (TBS pH 7.4, 1% NP-40, 5% glycerol and protease inhibitors) per well. The lysate was spun at 20,000g for 5 min. Next, 120 μl clarified lysate was saved as input whereas the rest was incubated protein G Sepharose beads (GE Healthcare) loaded with anti-NRF2 antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, 12721S) at 4 °C for 1 h. Afterwards, 2 µg NRF2 antibody was added to each sample. After incubation, the beads were washed 3 times with NP-40 lysis buffer, and bound proteins were eluted in 120 μl 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. Samples were heated to 95 °C for 20 min followed by separation by SDS–PAGE.

Sources indicate that cell culture supernatants were transferred into microcentrifuge tubes and depleted of cells and debris by centrifuging at 400g for 5 min. Peritoneal lavage fluid was prepared as described above. Equal volumes of cell-free supernatants or peritoneal lavage fluid were mixed with 0.5 µg biotinylated goat anti-mouse IL-1β or anti-human IL-1β antibody and 20 µl dry weight neutravidin agarose beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C while rotating, washed 3 times with PBS pH 7.4 and protein was eluted in 50 µl 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. The remaining cells in the well were lysed in 1× sample buffer and served as lysate control. Samples were heated to 65 °C for 10 min followed by separation by SDS–PAGE. IL-1β was detected by immunoblotting using Bio-Rad Image Lab. Cell-associated actin was detected as the loading control.

According to recent reports, for analysis of inflammasome activation in cells cultured on variable stiffness plates, primary mouse BMDMs were plated at 3 × 106 cells per well and cultured overnight. The medium was exchanged for OptiMEM (Gibco) and cells were left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 6 h or 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h followed by 5 mM ATP for 2 h. The cell culture supernatant was removed, cleared of debris by centrifugation at 400g for 5 min at room temperature and then protein was precipitated by adding trichloroacetic acid to a final concentration of 10%. Samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C while rotating, protein was pelleted by centrifugation at 13,000g at 4 °C for 15 min and was washed twice with 400 µl ice-cold acetone. Protein pellets were air dried at 65 °C for 5 min. Protein was solubilized in 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. The remaining cells in the well were lysed in 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME and served as lysate control. All samples were heated to 65 °C for 10 min followed by protein separation by SDS–PAGE.

In a recent development, for analysis of inflammasome activation in WT, Nfe2l2−/−, Keap1f/f and LysM-Cre;Keap1f/f primary BMDMs, 1 × 106 cells per well were plated in a 24-well dish and cultured overnight in cDMEM. For analysis of inflammasome activation in iBMDMs, 1 × 106 cells per well were plated in a 24-well dish and cultured for 1 h in cDMEM. Cells were then left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h, medium was removed and OptiMEM containing nigericin was added for 1–2 h. Cells and supernatant were lysed together by addition of 5× sample buffer containing 10% β-ME, lysates were needle homogenized and samples were heated to 95 °C for 5 min followed by protein separation by SDS–PAGE.

Primary mouse BMDMs from WT and Gsdmd−/− mice were plated at 3 × 106 cells per well in soft (2 kPa) or plastic plates and cultured overnight. The medium was exchanged for OptiMEM and cells were left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 6 h or 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h followed by 5 mM ATP for 2 h. Protein was precipitated as outlined above and solubilized in 1× sample buffer without reducing agent. Protein was solubilized by incubating at 65 °C for 5 min, after which samples were split equally into two tubes and β-ME or an equal volume of ddH2O was added to generate reducing and non-reducing samples, respectively. Whole-cell lysate was generated by adding 1× sample buffer to the remaining cells, solubilizing at 65 °C for 5 min, splitting the sample equally and adding either β-ME or an equal volume of ddH2O to generate reducing and non-reducing samples. The final concentration of β-ME was 2%. Proteins were separated by SDS–PAGE on a 4–12% acrylamide gradient gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and GSDMD was detected by western blotting. The assembled GSDMD pore is resistant to SDS under non-reducing conditions and thus oligomerization was indicated by a gel shift towards a higher molecular weight. Cell-associated actin was detected as the loading control.

In a recent development, fractionation was performed as previously described87. In brief, primary BMDMs derived from WT and Nfe2l2−/− mice were seeded in variable stiffness plates at 3 × 106 cells per well. A total of 3 wells were used per genotype and stiffness and BMDMs were cultured overnight. Cells were placed on ice and washed once with ice-cold PBS. Cells were scraped into ice cold PBS, spun at 10,000g for 10 s, and PBS was aspirated. Cells were lysed in 900 µl PBS, 0.1% NP-40 and protease inhibitors by trituration with a P1000 pipette. A total of 300 µl of this was saved as whole-cell lysate. The remaining 600 µl lysate was spun at 10,000g for 10 s and 300 µl of the supernatant was saved as the cytoplasmic fraction. Next, 75 µl of 5× sample buffer containing 10% β-ME was added to the whole-cell lysate and cytoplasmic fractions to denature the protein. The remaining supernatant was aspirated, and the nuclear pellet was washed with 1 ml PBS, 0.1% NP-40 and protease inhibitors. The nuclear pellet was lysed in 300 µl 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. All fractions were needle homogenized and then boiled at 100 °C for 5 min. Tubulin and lamin A/C served as markers for the cytosol and nucleus, respectively. Cell-associated actin was detected as the loading control.

It has been revealed that cells were seeded at 1 × 106 primary BMDMs per well in 6-well 2 kPa Cytosoft or plastic Petri dishes coated with fibronectin. One well was left without cells as a blank. Cells were cultured overnight in the presence or absence of NAC (5 mM, pH 7.4), MitoTempo (15 µM), ML171 (1 µM), GSK2795039 (10 µM) or GKT137831 (10 µM). The next morning, cells were incubated with 20 µM H2DCFDA in 1× HBSS without phenol red for 30 min. Cells were then washed 3 times with HBSS without phenol red and bottom read fluorescence was read using a TecanSpark with an excitation wavelength of 490 nm, emission wavelength of 535 nm and bandwidth of 20.0. Cells were then lysed in 350 µl RNA lysis buffer containing 1% β-ME and stored at −20 °C until further processing.

In a recent development, iBMDMs were seeded on glass coverslips at 2.5 × 105 cells per well in 24-well dishes and left to adhere for 1 h. Primary BMDMs were seeded on glass coverslips at 1 × 105 cells per well in 24-well dishes in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants, left to adhere overnight. The next morning, medium was removed and replaced with cDMEM. Cells were stimulated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h, after which medium was aspirated and replaced with 450 µl OptiMEM containing zVAD-FMK with or without nigericin for 30 min. Cells were fixed by the addition of 150 µl of 16% EM-grade aqueous paraformaldehyde (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were washed twice with PBS pH 7.4 and stored overnight at 4 °C. The next morning, cells were permeabilized and blocked for 30 min in PBS pH 7.4 containing 0.2% BSA and 0.05% saponin (blocking buffer). Cells were washed 3 times in PBS pH 7.4 and primary antibody staining was performed for 1 h in blocking buffer containing polyclonal rabbit anti-ASC antibody (Adipogen) at 1:100 dilution in a humidified chamber. Cells were washed 5 times in PBS pH 7.4 and secondary antibody staining was performed for 1 h in blocking buffer containing Alexa Fluor 488-tagged polyclonal goat anti-rabbit IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a 1:200 dilution, Alexa Fluor 647-tagged phalloidin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 1:400 dilution and DAPI (Biotum) at 1 µg ml–1 in a humidified chamber in the dark. Cells were washed 5–10 times in PBS pH 7.4, mounted on glass slides using prolong glass antifade mountant (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and left to cure overnight at room temperature in the dark. Images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM 880 with Airyscan and processed using Zeiss Zen Blue (v.2.3SP1). ASC specks were manually counted, and nuclei were counted in Fiji (v.2.16.0) using the Analyze particles algorithm.

Sources indicate that tissue samples for these experiments were isolated from discarded explanted human lung tissue specimens collected at Massachusetts General Hospital. Patients provided informed consent, and discarded tissue samples from non-diseased donors were collected under Massachusetts General Hospital IRB number 2016P001890. Discarded tissue from patients with ILD were collected under Massachusetts General Hospital IRB number 2013P002332. Samples were fixed in 4% buffered paraformaldehyde and then embedded in paraffin. The following primary antibodies were used for immunofluorescence: monoclonal mouse anti-human CD68 (Abcam, ab955), polyclonal rabbit anti-human SLC7A11 (Abcam, ab37185), polyclonal rabbit anti-human HMOX1 (Proteintech, 10701-1-AP) and polyclonal rabbit anti-human GSR (Proteintech, 18257-1-AP). Paraffin-embedded tissue was sectioned at 5 µm slices onto glass slides, deparaffinized and then rehydrated. Antigen retrieval was performed using Tris-EDTA pH 9 for 5 min in a pressure cooker, after which samples were cooled and tissue was circled using a hydrophobic pen. Sections were permeabilized and blocked using sterile filtered PBS, 1% BSA and 0.3% Triton X-100 (blocking-staining buffer). Sections were stained with primary antibody at 4 °C overnight at the following dilutions: CD68, 1:100; HMOX1, 1:50; GSR, 1:50; and SLC7A11, 1:100. Sections were washed 5 times in blocking–staining buffer and then left in blocking–staining buffer for 10 min. Secondary antibody staining was performed at room temperature in blocking–staining buffer containing Alexa Fluor 594-tagged polyclonal goat anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor 647-tagged polyclonal goat anti-mouse IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 1:400) along with Hoechst (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 1:2,000) for 2 h. Samples were then washed 5 times with blocking–staining buffer, submerged in PBS pH 7.4 and 0.1% Triton X-100 for 30 min, dipped in deionized water and mounted with Fluoromount-G mounting medium (Southern Biotech). Samples were imaged on a Zeiss Axio Imager.M2 widefield microscope and a Zeiss LSM 780 confocal microscope.

According to recent reports, cells were detected using Cellpose (v.2.0) and the implemented model ‘Cellpose fluorescence’ (CP) with the following parameters: average cell diameter 50 pixels (12.2 µm), flow threshold 2.0 and cell probability threshold –3. Segmentation was performed on the stained cells using nuclei as a secondary channel for detection. The resulting labels were filtered for a minimum size of 600 pixels (35.4 µm2), and the resulting labels were used to calculate fluorescence values of the corresponding cells. An empirically determined threshold for the average CD68 fluorescence intensity was used to discriminate alveolar macrophages from interstitial macrophages and stromal cells following histogram normalization of the underlying imaging data. The mean fluorescence intensity and sum of fluorescence per cell were plotted in PRISM (GraphPad).

Industry observers note that BMDMs were grown on Cytosoft 2 kPa plates or glass cover slips, both coated with fibronectin as described above. BMDMs were immersion-fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences), 2% paraformaldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences) and 0.3% picric acid (Sigma-Aldrich) in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate (Sigma-Aldrich) pH 7.4 for 1 h at room temperature. BMDMs were washed with 0.1 M sodium cacodylate and then post-fixed for 1 h at 4 °C in 1% osmium tetroxide (Electron Microscopy Sciences) in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate. BMDMs were then washed in DI water and incubated in 2% aqueous uranyl acetate (Electron Microscopy Sciences) overnight at 4 °C. The following day, BMDMs were washed with DI water and then dehydrated at 4 °C in a graded ethanol series. BMDMs were then brought to room temperature and dehydrated with 100% ethanol (Sigma-Aldrich). Infiltration with LX112 resin (Ladd Research) was followed by embedding in flat-bottom Beem capsules (Electron Microscopy Sciences) cut to form a cylindrical mould on the growing substrate. The resulting blocks were separated from the culture plates using liquid nitrogen and then sectioned using a Leica Ultracut E ultramicrotome (Leica Microsystems). Sections were then placed on formvar and carbon-coated grids (Electron Microscopy Sciences). The sections were contrast stained with 2% uranyl acetate followed by lead citrate (Sigma-Aldrich) and imaged in a Jeol 1400 transmission electron microscope (Jeol) equipped with a Gatan Orius SC1000 digital CCD camera (Gatan). Mitochondrial length was manually measured in Fiji (v.2.16.0).

It has been revealed that RNA was isolated using a PureLink RNA Mini kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). In brief, cells were collected in lysis buffer containing 1% β-ME and stored frozen at −20 °C until processing. Equal volumes of 70% ethanol were added to each sample, which were then applied to PureLink RNA columns and processed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Total RNA was eluted using 50 µl RNAse-free H2O. RT–qPCR was performed using a Taqman RNA-to-Ct 1-step kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on equal amounts of RNA per the manufacturer’s protocol. The following Taqman probes were used: Gsta3 (Mm00494798_m1), Nqo1 (Mm01253561_m1), Gsr (Mm00439154_m1), Hmox1 (Mm00516005_m1), Gclm (Mm01324400_m1), Slc7a11 (Mm00442530_m1), Srxn1 (Mm00769566_m1), Txnrd1 (Mm00443675_m1), Nfe2l2 (Mm00477784_m1), Keap1 (Mm00497268_m1), Il1b (Mm00434228_m1), Panx1 (Mm00450900_m1), Il6 (Mm00446190_m1), Nos2 (Mm00440502_m1), Arg1 (Mm00475988_m1), Retnla (Mm00445109_m1), Nox1 (Mm00549170_m1), Cybb (Mm01287743_m1) and Tbp (Mm01277042_m1). Data were normalized to Tbp, analysed using Microsoft Excel and plotted in GraphPad Prism.

Recent findings suggest that for determination of Nfe2l2 deletion, RNA was collected purified from cells using a PureLink RNA Mini kit (Life Technologies) and PureLink DNase I (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The quality and quantity of RNA were assessed using a Nanodrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). cDNA was synthesized from 1 μg RNA using a High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription kit (Applied Biosystems). Gene expression was analysed by qPCR using a SYBR Green gene expression assay (Applied Biosystems) and primers were synthesized from IDT. The following mouse Nfe2l2 primer sequences were used: forward 5′-TAGATGACCATGAGTCGCTTGC-3′, reverse 5′-GCCAAACTTGCTCCATGTCC-3′. The following mouse cyclophilin B primer sequences were used: forward 5′-AGCATACAGGTCCTGGCATC-3′, reverse 5′- TTCACCTTCCCAAAGACCAC-3′. Sources indicate that BMDMs were seeded at 1 × 106 cells per well in 6-well Cytosoft or plastic Petri dishes coated with fibronectin and cultured overnight. Cells were washed once with PBS, collected in lysis buffer containing 1% β-ME and stored frozen at −80 °C until processing. RNA was processed using the QIAsymphony RNA protocol according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, RNA was extracted using QIAsymphony RNA Isolation kits (Qiagen) on a QIAsymphony SP instrument using the RNA CT 400 protocol. The elution volume for RNA samples was 100 µl. RNA sequencing libraries were constructed from 500 ng total RNA using a KAPA RNA HyperPrep kit (Kapa Biosystems). Library preparation was tested manually and subsequently fully automated on a Biomek i7 Workstation (Beckmen Coulter). Libraries underwent paired-end 75 base-pair sequencing on a NovaSeq6000 (Illumina) at a depth of 50 million reads per sample. Raw reads were aligned to the mouse genome (GRCm39) using the STAR aligner (v.-2.7.5c). Reads mapped to genomic features were counted using the FeatureCounts function from the subread package (v.1.6.0). The count matrix was imported into R (v.4.1.3) and low-expressed genes were filtered out (included genes required ≥1 CPM in at least 20% of samples). Trimmed mean of M-values was computed using edgeR (v.3.38.0). Differential gene expression analysis was computed using the limma package (v.3.52.0). Differentially expressed genes were loaded into ingenuity pathway analysis (Qiagen, v.01-22-01) and upstream regulator and canonical pathway analysis was conducted on samples with an absolute value log2 fold change > 1 and a corrected P < 0.05. Heatmaps were generated using ComplexHeatmap (v.2.18.0).

Recent findings suggest that for effects of stiffness on the NRF2 transcriptional program, WT and Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs were seeded at 1 × 106 cells per well in soft (2 kPa) or plastic 6-well dishes in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants and incubated overnight. For the effect of NRF2 activators on LPS-stimulated transcription, WT and Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs were seeded at 1 × 106 cells per well in 12-well TC dishes in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants and incubated overnight. The next morning, medium was replaced with fresh cDMEM containing 1 µM KI696, 5 µM sulforaphane, 100 µM tert-butylhydroquinone, 25 µM dimethyl fumarate, 125 µM 4-octyl itaconate or DMSO as a control, and BMDMs were incubated for 30 min. Half of the cells were left unstimulated and the other half had LPS added to a final concentration of 100 ng ml–1 and were cultured for 6 h.

In a recent development, for all samples, supernatants were aspirated and cells were lysed in 350 µl RNA Lysis buffer from a PureLink RNA kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). RNA was isolated as described in the RT–qPCR section above. Technical triplicates were combined to create one sample per condition per mouse, DNA was degraded using a TURBO DNA-free kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and RNA was quantified using a Nanodrop instrument. RNA was kept frozen at −80 °C and paired-end 150 base-pair sequencing was conducted by Azenta at a depth of 20 million reads per sample. Raw sequencing data processing was done with the Galaxy server, whereas differential gene expression analysis was performed in R (v.4.3.2). Raw reads were trimmed using fastp (Galaxy v.0.23.2) and aligned to the mouse genome (mm10) using RNA STAR aligner (Galaxy v.2.7.11a). Reads mapped to genomic features were counted using FeatureCounts (Galaxy v.2.0.3). Differential gene expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 (v.1.42.0) and heatmaps were generated using ComplexHeatmap (v.2.18.0).

WT BMDMs were cultured for 5 days in 2% CMG, then left untreated or treated with RANKL to generate osteoclasts. On day 5, cells were treated with or without 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 3 h. RNA was extracted using a PureLink RNA Mini kit (Invitrogen) with on-column DNase treatment (Ambion). RNA quality and quantity were assessed using an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Libraries were prepared using a NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep kit and sequenced on an Illumina platform to generate paired end reads. Raw reads were cleaned using fastp and aligned to the reference genome, mm10 using STAR. Gene expression was quantified with Feature Counts, and RPKM values were calculated. Differential expression was analysed using DESeq2 with Benjamini–Hochberg correction (adjusted P < 0.05). Heatmaps were generated using ComplexHeatmap. Three biological replicates were used per group.

Spatial transcriptomic data from human lung tissue were downloaded from the NIH Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) platform (identifier GSE250346)79, whereas single-cell RNA sequencing data were downloaded from NIH GEO (identifiers GSE122960 and GSE136831)80,81. All analyses were performed using Seurat (v.5.0.1). Data from ref. 80 (GSE122960) required integration, which was performed using the IntegrateLayers pipeline in Seurat. Data from ref. 81 (GSE136831) were available as a sparse matrix and a Seurat object was manually created using these data. Data from ref. 79 (GSE250346) were available as a Seurat object. In brief, cells were re-clustered and individual cluster annotations were confirmed manually. NRF2 transcriptional targets were used to generate an NRF2 module score across all cell types using the AddModuleScore. The NRF2 activity score was then compared between samples from unaffected individuals and samples with more fibrosis on a per-macrophage-subtype basis. Significance was assessed using the Kruskal–Wallis test and Dunn’s multiple comparisons test, and P values were adjusted using Bonferroni correction. Violin plots were generated using scCustomize (v.2.0.1). Pseudobulk analysis was performed by creating an aggregated count matrix followed by differential gene expression analysis using DESeq2 (v.1.42.0). Normalized counts were extracted and GSVA (v.1.50.0) was performed using NRF2 target genes as the target gene set. Significance was assessed using the Mann–Whitney U-test. All data analyses were performed using R (v.4.3.2).

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend with a growing treatment table and a lot of questions for Xabi Alonso to answer before Saturday’s visit of Bournemouth.

The main concern revolves around Joao Pedro. Chelsea’s current player of the season rescued a point against newly promoted Hull, but he suffered a knock and sat out the damaging 3-0 defeat at Brentford. The problem also prompted his removal from Brazil’s squad shortly after he had returned to it.

It has been revealed that it is understood that he is undergoing specialist knee treatment in an attempt to expedite his recovery, although reports in Brazil suggest that he could be out for up to four weeks. No date has yet been set, but a return later in October looks most likely.

Sources indicate that there is more good news elsewhere. Cole Palmer was among the players called up to the latest England squad, which did not go down too well with Thomas Tuchel.

Sources indicate that the midfielder has been recovering from a persistent groin injury and has been working with a rehab coach. He is likely to be fit this weekend.

According to recent reports, moises Caicedo has also struggled with an injury this season, playing just 14 minutes across the campaign. He’s spent the majority of time on the bench recovering from a bad calf injury, which ruled him out for most of the season.

He made his only appearance as a substitute against his former club Brighton, but the game was red-flagged for Ecuador’s friendlies, so he did not play.

In a recent development, alonso said before the Brentford match that the player would be ready to return. It seems to be the case, unless something went wrong.

Sources indicate that captain Reece James missed the Brentford game with yet another hamstring problem. Alonso said he only just missed out, so a return seems likely.

It has been revealed that there may also be debuts. Marco Palestra, the £27m signing from Atalanta, has been sidelined since a training injury just before the opening match against Fulham. He is back in full training and was expected to feature in a behind-closed-doors friendly with Portsmouth. Chelsea lost 2-0. Emmanuel Emegha, injured after scoring against Bromley in July, is also pushing for involvement.

In a recent development, less clear is the position of Jamie Gittens. He limped off with an ankle injury playing for England Under-21s against Kazakhstan and was seen on crutches. Mike Penders is fine after a quad scare on Belgium duty. Returning to the bench against Turkey.

Chelsea badly need a lift. Defeat at Brentford before the break left Alonso’s side looking shaky, and a squad stretched by injuries has not helped.

Recent findings suggest that saturday brings a chance to steady things. If Palmer, James and Caicedo are available, with Palestra and Emegha potentially adding fresh options, the picture will look much brighter at Stamford Bridge. Joao Pedro’s absence will still sting. However, a strong response against Bournemouth would go a long way towards easing the pressure and restoring belief.

Viktor Gyökeres has put to bed any doubts over his future at Arsenal by stating his desire to stay.

Gyökeres moved to Arsenal for £63.5m from Sporting Lisbon last summer. He’s played a key role in the club winning the Premier League last season with 14 league goals.

However, he has not featured as much this season. Kai Havertz often being Arteta’s go-to man centrally, resulting in him only starting once in the Premier League.

Gyökeres was asked if he wants to stay at Arsenal and has made it clear he wants to continue his career at the Emirates.

The striker also spoke about his relationship with Arteta.

He explained that they regularly discuss football, the team’s approach and the opposition. Those conversations also help him understand what Arteta expects when he is selected to start.

It is a key point to note that just because he hasn’t had much time on the pitch doesn’t mean there have been any challenges between the two.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Laurence Stewart is set to leave Chelsea by mutual consent after almost four years at Stamford Bridge, with the club opting to redistribute his responsibilities rather than appoint a direct replacement.
  • According to recent reports, the departure is understood to be amicable and won’t take immediate effect.
  • The story was first reported by Matt Law of The Telegraph and Nizaar Kinsella of BBC Sport, with Ben Jacobs subsequently providing further details about how Chelsea intend to operate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Laurence Stewart is set to leave Chelsea by mutual consent after almost four years at Stamford Bridge, with the club opting to redistribute his responsibilities rather than appoint a direct replacement.

According to recent reports, the departure is understood to be amicable and won’t take immediate effect. Stewart could continue attending matches before formally leaving, following discussions with co-owner Behdad Eghbali over the club’s evolving sporting structure.

The story was first reported by Matt Law of The Telegraph and Nizaar Kinsella of BBC Sport, with Ben Jacobs subsequently providing further details about how Chelsea intend to operate.

Stewart arrived from Monaco in October 2022 as technical director before becoming co-sporting director alongside Paul Winstanley in February 2023.

Chelsea’s day-to-day sporting leadership will now be shared between Winstanley, Sam Jewell and Joe Shields, each with defined responsibilities.

It has been revealed that winstanley will continue overseeing transfer negotiations, player contracts and several departments at Cobham, including medical and performance operations. Shields’ work centres on the academy and player pathways, while Jewell has wider responsibilities across the BlueCo operation, including Strasbourg.

According to Jacobs, discussions about restructuring began in April and accelerated following the appointment of Xabi Alonso as head coach.

Stewart had overseen investment in Chelsea’s data analysis operation, although Jewell and Shields have increasingly taken responsibility for using that information in recruitment and talent identification.

Dave Fallows will remain involved in an advisory capacity, rather than taking on a fixed day-to-day portfolio.

The changes are being described as a natural evolution of Chelsea’s sporting model. There is no suggestion that Stewart’s departure followed a breakdown in relations, and the club are not presently planning to recruit a replacement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Matteo Gabbia has admitted that he could return to the field in January for AC Milan, but he doesn’t want to rush back.

Industry observers note that it has been a difficult season for Milan, at least where injuries are concerned. In defence, they have had concerns reminiscent of the 2023/24 season, where Gabbia had to be brought back from his loan spell at Villarreal.

According to recent reports, read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Industry observers note that this season, though, it seems Gerry Cardinale is going to go down a different route and spend to help Ruben Amorim with his defensive options. Indeed, there have been plenty of rumours about recruitments at the back.

However, Gabbia could again be a key returnee in January, with him hoping to return from injury early in the new year.

Speaking to Sky Sport (via MilanNews) – at an event organised by the Milan Foundation at Milan’s “Arturo Toscanini” secondary school, where they met with several children with disabilities – Gabbia discussed the importance of the event, as well as his recovery.

What were the emotions of this meeting?

“It’s wonderful, very enjoyable to spend hours with them. It’s also beautiful to see how they manage to create a group, something that really shows the importance of teamwork, the importance of friendship, even among themselves.

“We’re happy; we thank Fondazione Milan for the project, which is always beautiful and important: we’re happy to be a part of it and we’re enjoying the afternoon.”.

Are you able to rejoin the group in January?

Recent findings suggest that “Yes, that could be the time: we’re trying to work hard and do everything as best we can. I obviously have to thank the physiotherapists and the doctor because we’re really doing everything we can every day to try to heal the injury and get back on the pitch feeling good.

“It’s definitely been an unlucky season for me so far: I don’t want it to happen again or for any recurrences, so it’s also notable to take the right time, get back in shape, and support the team right now.”.

“Although it’s bad for the team that there are so many injured players, we’re together right now, supporting each other and trying to encourage each other through therapy, gym work, and the entire recovery process. Therefore, we’re trying to work as a team this week too, to overcome all the players’ injuries.

“From a personal standpoint, I’m trying to take this time calmly, in the sense that these things are part of sport, part of life, and not all moments are the same.

“This is certainly a difficult time, but it still allows me to stay close to the team, to try to lend my support, even in the good and bad times. That’s what I’m doing, in addition to obviously doing what I can to try to return as soon as possible and make my contribution on the pitch.”.

How do you explain the team’s ups and downs?

“I think it’s something we need to get our heads around; we need to understand the importance of every game.

In a recent development, “The other day I heard our coach give an interview in which he said something vital: we need to understand that every game, when you don’t win, is taken as a defeat, a heavy defeat. We need to truly understand the importance of every game and approach training to prepare 100%, as best as possible, for every match.

“Therefore, I think this is room for improvement, but I see a group that is really eager to improve, to work, and as a result, I’m sure we’ll be able to fix this flaw as well.

“Although we’ve had a good start to the year in the league and less so in the Europa League, we have plenty of time to improve and have a strong year.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Premier League goalkeeper Jussi Jääskeläinen thinks David Raya is the best goalkeeper in the division right now.

But the former Bolton Wanderers star feels the Arsenal No.1 has more to prove before he can be put up with the all-time greats of the competition.

Jääskeläinen recently spoke to Kasinopartio.com, where he praised Raya’s performances and the understanding he has developed with Arsenal’s defenders.

“Raya has been a fantastic signing. He has a great relationship with the centre-backs; even when the back four changes, everything works well.”.

The Spaniard has played a key role for Mikel Arteta since his arrival from Brentford. His organisation of the backline, key saves and contribution to Arsenal’s build up play have helped him to be a standout player.

In 2012, Raya began his journey in English football when he moved to Blackburn Rovers from Spain. At that time, he was just a young teenager unfamiliar with English football.

His short spell at Southport introduced him to senior football. Soon, he returned to Blackburn and forged a career ahead of moving to Brentford in 2019. After four years with Brentford, Raya achieved success at the club, helping them to the Premier League.

The player’s performances in the higher leagues caught the attention of Arsenal, and Arteta signed him on loan to the Emirates in 2023 before making the move permanent the following summer.

Sources indicate that it didn’t take long for Raya to establish himself in the team. He took home the Premier League Golden Glove, having achieved 16 clean sheets in 32 appearances.

This was a significant milestone in his first season with the Arsenal team, and he has since remained as number one, playing a key role in the club’s pursuit of titles.

While Jääskeläinen said Raya is the best goalkeeper in the Premier League at the moment, he does not think he should be up there with the most experienced.

He believes other goalkeepers have earned an advantage through their consistency over a longer period.

“You have lots of top goalkeepers that I think are still a little bit ahead because of the years they’ve done it in the Premier League.”.

“He’s not up there with them yet, but he’s definitely going in the right direction.”.

It has been revealed that raya has already proven he can play to the top standard. However, it will be his consistency moving forward that will define his long-term reputation.

It has been revealed that petr Čech, Peter Schmeichel and Edwin van der Sar have all gained great reputations over the years. There is still plenty of time for Raya to do the same, but he will need to keep up his high standards whilst wearing an Arsenal shirt.

At just 31, Raya has a lot left in his career. If he can continue playing at this level, it will make the debate around whether he is one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League even more intriguing.

There’ll be some relief amongst the West Ham medical staff at Rush Green tonight knowing that Manor Solomon was left out of Israel’s match altogether after the winger could not train owing to the pain of an ongoing injury.

However there will be concern that this same glitch which dogged Solomon through September might yet prevent him playing his full part in the busy run up to Christmas  – with its demanding schedule of nine games in a little over a month.

Solomon came back from the last international break in September looking washed out, and in truth, his performances since have been a disappointment after his early season impact and man-of-the-match award.

Solomon – early season form has fallen away as his back injury has made itself known.

There’s been a sneaking suspicion that Solomon has been playing with an injury -and this would seem to be confirmed by his being left out of his national side. In truth he probably should not even have travelled. According to Yahoo Sports:.

“The winger missed out on the Israel squad completely for the 0-0 draw with Kosovo on Saturday.

Solomon had been suffering from back challenges, and only partially trained on Wednesday.

He participated in the first session, before missing the second one and then tried to train on Friday.

However, Israeli boss Ran Ben-Shimon confirmed that he was in too much pain, and ultimately left him out of the contest.”.

From a purely selfish club vs country perspective, West Ham could really do with the winger sitting out Israel’s next fixture against Austria on Tuesday evening.

Whilst Edvin Austbø has pulled ahead of Solomon in the pecking order, I shouldn’t wonder if Solomon’s back problems have been affecting him ever since he arrived at London Stadium and as the hours on the pitch have racked up, his high-energy output has nose dived.

There will be no live UK television coverage of Chelsea’s return to Premier League action against Bournemouth on Saturday afternoon.

Xabi Alonso’s side host the Cherries at Stamford Bridge in a traditional 3pm kick-off, with the fixture falling within the Saturday afternoon broadcasting blackout.

That means supporters unable to attend will need to follow the match through other channels, rather than watching it live on Sky Sports or TNT Sports.

Although the game will not be televised live in the UK, supporters can follow developments through the official Chelsea website and the Premier League website.

The Saturday 3pm blackout prevents live domestic television broadcasts during the restricted period, although overseas coverage may be available through broadcasters holding the relevant rights.

Highlights will be available after the match through the usual broadcast and digital channels, subject to their respective release schedules.

Chelsea will then turn their attention to a trip to Everton on Saturday, 17 October, with that fixture scheduled for a 12.30pm kick-off at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

For Alonso, the Bournemouth match provides the immediate opportunity to resume Chelsea’s domestic campaign following the international break.

England's Euro 2028 mission starts NOW! Thomas Tuchel's men must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - or risk their 'DNA' cursing them yet again, writes OLIVER HOLT

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 16:10 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • It is four months, almost to the day, since England shrank from the call of history and lost their World Cup semi-final to Argentina in Atlanta but Thomas Tuchel may not believe that the Nations League tie against Spain in the Metropolitano on Sunday evening represents his best shot at redemption for the way things played out that afternoon in America’s South.
  • That is largely because Tuchel does not appear to believe he has anything to redeem himself for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By OLIVER HOLT, CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 16:10 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 14 November 2026.

It is four months, almost to the day, since England shrank from the call of history and lost their World Cup semi-final to Argentina in Atlanta but Thomas Tuchel may not believe that the Nations League tie against Spain in the Metropolitano on Sunday evening represents his best shot at redemption for the way things played out that afternoon in America’s South.

That is largely because Tuchel does not appear to believe he has anything to redeem himself for. The manner of his side’s capitulation - and the substitutions he made - in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium last July enraged the nation, but Tuchel remarked the fault was in the damned DNA of the English, that we were underlings, and that our players found it constitutionally impossible to keep hold of the ball.

Whatever Tuchel thinks, the fact remains that the tie against Lamine Yamal, Fabian Ruiz, Pedri and Mikel Oyarzabal and the rest of the world champions at the home of Atletico Madrid offers Tuchel and his players the opportunity to encourage themselves and their fans that they are not destined to be also-rans wired to fall at the final hurdle for evermore.

Industry observers note that spain are formidable opposition. They are on a record-breaking run of 43 matches unbeaten and have won their last 12 in succession. They haven't drawn a game since their June 15 game against Cape Verde in the World Cup. Their last defeat was on March 22, 2024, when they lost 1-0 to Colombia in a friendly. Some ask whether they are the best international side the world has ever seen.

‘Spain seem unbeatable,’ Tuchel noted, when he walked into the press room at the Metropolitano on Saturday night and heard hymns of praise being lavished upon the opponents he is about to face.

It has been revealed that ‘They have a very strong identity and a very strong mentality. We are trying to take it away from them. We are up for it. We are up for the fight. We are up for a spectacular match. We can see how far we can push the limits with the world champions in Madrid. The group is full of self-belief and rightly so.’.

England must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - even if they have flaws.

Thomas Tuchel must show he can find a way around the limitations presented by the 'DNA' he has complained about.

Recent findings suggest that this may be the toughest game that Tuchel’s England side play until the European Championships in 2028, where the final will be contested at Wembley, and they will play all their games at home. They need to go into that tournament with the belief that they can beat the best when the pressure is at its highest.

Industry observers note that beating Spain away in the final game of the group phase of the Nations League is not quite the same as a critical match at a major tournament but it is as stiff a challenge as Tuchel is going to face until then. Beating Croatia 7-0 in front of gangs of schoolkids in Rijeka last month was hailed as the best England performance of the Tuchel era. Which says it all, really.

Recent findings suggest that it was a great performance in a relatively meaningless match. Now it is time for him to show that he can marshal an England side to succeed against the very best, not fall apart when the prize is in sight. His protestations of powerlessness in the aftermath of the Argentina defeat were not a good look for a coach who was hired with the idea that his coaching prowess and his game management could get England over the line.

It has been revealed that has he learned anything from the manner of the Argentina defeat? ‘This game against Spain will be proof of concept at the highest level,’ he noted, ‘but we are up for it. I think we have taken the next step after the World Cup. The best thing is to trust our process and trust ourselves. We need to be clear about how we want to impose ourselves and I think that is all visible.’.

Now it is time for him to show that he can find a way past the limitations of England’s footballing DNA, find a way to compete with Spain and France when it really matters, and find a way to end the culture of near misses that has come to be England’s lot in the last decade of appearances in semi-finals and finals.

England have played six matches since that day of crushing disappointment in Atlanta and scored 22 goals. But in the only one of those matches that really mattered, they lost 3-2 to Spain at Wembley in the opening tie of their Nations League campaign at the end of September, a game in which they were largely outclassed by Luis de la Fuente’s team.

In a recent development, spain are what England have to aim for. Tuchel mentioned their example and their ability and their mindset straight after the semi-final loss to Argentina. ‘Ball possession plays a crucial role,’ he noted at his post-match press conference in Atlanta. ‘It’s maybe not in our DNA like it is in our Spanish DNA or in our Argentinian-Brazilian DNA, to take the ball and control the game with the ball.’.

This may well be their toughest game until the final of the 2028 European Championships, if they get that far.

The England coach said more recently that England need to go back to trusting a traditional style that emphasises direct, high-intensity physicality rather than trying to copy Spanish patience in ball-retention. England, though, were taught a lesson in sophistication by the Spanish in September.

According to recent reports, and for all the attention lavished on Yamal, Spain’s defence is the best in the world. Rodri, the shield for that defence and also the world’s best in the role, is not fit for this game but even without him, Spain’s back-line inspires an awful lot more confidence than England’s.

It has been revealed that ‘They were the best in the World Cup at the back,’ Declan Rice, England’s central midfielder, mentioned on Saturday. ‘Defence wins you titles. Everyone talks about their attacking talent but you look at their central defenders, their full backs and the way their midfielders contribute to the defence, too.’.

That defence will have to stop England’s resurgent front line, led by Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane, who could be flanked by Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers and backed up by the supreme talent of Jude Bellingham just behind them.

Bellingham’s improving relationship with Tuchel, which cannot have been harmed by the inclusion of Bellingham’s brother, Jobe, in this squad, is another reason to hope that England still retain the capacity to improve after the World Cup. The elder Bellingham has become England’s most influential player.

According to recent reports, england at their best would be one of the few teams capable of extending them. Rice said on Saturday that the game between the two sides was ‘massive’. England need to prove they can find a way to get closer to the world champions. To beat them, Rice said, would be a ‘massive statement’.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Playing against them is a great incentive to win. It will show where we are as a group. We are trying to attack teams full throttle and with players like Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers in our attack, it feels as if it is going to take off one night and maybe tomorrow night will be the night. We can beat Spain. For sure, we can.’.

Industry observers note that tuchel needs to prove England can win, not just be noble contenders. They need to prove that their DNA need not be a curse.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bournemouth’s determination to keep Alex Scott has done little to discourage Chelsea, who remain among the leading contenders to sign the England midfielder.

Sources indicate that the Blues had a £64m bid rejected during the summer, but their interest has continued into the new season. According to Matt Law of The Telegraph, Chelsea are at the front of the queue of clubs monitoring the 23-year-old.

Bournemouth, however, have no intention of allowing Scott to leave in January. talkSPORT reported this week that the south coast club remain determined to retain him, despite his reluctance to sign a contract extension.

Scott’s current deal runs until 2028, leaving Bournemouth with time to negotiate, although their position could become more complicated if no agreement is reached before next summer.

It has been revealed that the midfielder’s immediate priority is recovering from a thigh injury sustained while representing England. He impressed during the 7-0 Nations League victory over Croatia but was withdrawn after 70 minutes. Subsequent examinations revealed a quadriceps problem, with BBC Sport reporting that he could miss six to eight weeks.

Sources indicate that his absence is a setback for Bournemouth, who have relied heavily on the former Bristol City midfielder this season. It also introduces another consideration for clubs monitoring his progress ahead of the January window.

Chelsea are not alone in their admiration. Arsenal and Liverpool have also been linked with Scott, whose performances have attracted attention beyond the Premier League.

Suggestions circulating on social media that Bournemouth have already agreed to let him leave in January remain unsubstantiated. There has been no reliable confirmation of such an arrangement, and the club’s reported position is firmly against a winter sale.

For Chelsea, the more realistic opportunity may come next summer, particularly if Scott continues to resist signing a newly introduced contract.

There’s been another twist in the chaotic career of one of West Ham’s standout signings of the Tim Steidten era.

It would be fair to say that Jean Clair Todibo was largely unknown to Hammers fans when Tim Stediten whisked the former Barca defender to east London in his private jet for a VIP welcome in the summer of 2024.

Sadly its would also be fair to say that the defender has been part of a chaotic two and a half years during which he’s seen three West Ham managers – and fallen out with all of them – and declared himself unwilling to play for the club again.

Todibo – dressing room chaos never seems far away.

Chaos appears to have followed Todibo to France when West Ham finally – gratefully – found a loan destination for their unhappy defender in the summer as Todibo was sent to Lens owing to his desire (apparently) to work with manager Dino Toppmoller.

No sooner had the wayward West Ham defender landed than Toppmoller was fired – and his successor Yannick Cahuzac fared little better, lasting just two months.

Todibo is surely the only player in the Lens dressing room who will have played under six managers in side three years, as his newly introduced head coach is revealed as Didier Digard.

Scott Parker can’t have missed the fact that Todibo is due to return to east London at the end of the season – putting the defender on course to test Parker’s own managerial credentials when his loan ends next May. And few West Ham fans will welcome him back after his turbulent and truculent career in Claret and Blue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben White returned to the England senior squad on Thursday night but received a hostile reception at Wembley.

The Arsenal defender came on as a substitute in the 78th minute of England’s 2-1 Nations League win against Croatia but was met with boos from a section of the crowd.

Sources indicate that thomas Tuchel has since defended White, stating that he should be in the squad. However, this raises questions as to why some England supporters have turned on the defender after he has continued to perform well for Arsenal.

The answer lies with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

White left the England World Cup camp in November 2022, returning home due to personal reasons. The FA confirmed that White will not return to the squad and asked that his privacy be respected.

He did not play in the first two group games for England and missed the last group game against Wales due to illness.

There were reports that White had fallen out with assistant manager Steve Holland, but neither the FA nor England management confirmed this was the reason he left.

Gareth Southgate later stated there were no problems between White and Holland and that White had simply withdrawn himself from selection after the tournament.

This meant that White would never play for England again while Southgate was still manager. Some fans were clearly upset by this, as they felt White was shunning his country.

It has been revealed that when White returned under Tuchel in March 2026, he was met with a negative reaction. He was booed by the crowd when he scored his first-ever international goal against Uruguay. White was also booed in the same fashion against Japan.

Industry observers note that he has since explained that supporters might view the situation differently if they knew the full story. However, he has chosen not to reveal the private details behind his departure.

Tuchel has shown little concern about White being affected by the controversy.

The England boss said after the win on Thursday that he had not heard any boos and praised White’s qualities, work ethic and desire to play for his country.

He believes White can help England win games and added that he has the backing of the coaching staff.

Arsenal fans will be unsurprised to learn that White is still a valuable asset for Mikel Arteta, offering defensive consistency and being able to play as a right or centre-back.

The bad press that White is receiving from England fans will not go away any time soon. However, he has not done anything to hurt his reputation at club level. The reasons why he left for the World Cup are personal.

The main focus for Arsenal will be getting him match fit again. As for the England fans, we shall see.

#14656. UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
