There must be a sense of disappointment amongst West Ham’s academy that one of their much-heralded strikers, poached from north of the border in July 2025, hasn’t yet progressed on a more impressive trajectory.

After all, Daniel Cummings joined West Ham as the latest nineteen year old striker ‘wonderkid’ with Champions League experience having featured in Celtic’s European campaign before quitting the club and heading for east London last summer.

Sending the young forward out on loan to fifth-tier Aldershot Town (no disrespect to Aldershot) could be seen as West Ham’s tacit admission that the striker has not yet delivered on the precocious talent he displayed in Celtic’s youth team scoring, seemingly, at will.

After all, West Ham academy contemporary Josh Landers headed on loan to Scottish Championship side Ayr United – not exactly the Premier League either – but more challenging surely than the Vanarama National League in which Cummings now finds himself.

Fellow academy Scot Josh Landers is at Ayr United on loan.

It has been revealed that of course, there’s a certain amount of schadenfreude from his old club. Celtic fan site celticshorts.com proclaim with glee the apparent stalling of Cummings’ progress:.

“Grass is seldom greener after leaving Celtic – Daniel Cummings heads to Aldershot Town…From playing in Champions League at Villa Park for Celtic to Aldershot Town”.

Which Cummings will just have to deal with, get his head down, score some goals and answer the criticism from his former club in the best possible way.

In case they hadn’t noticed, now more than ever there’s an opening back at home for any young striker who creates a splash and one or other of Landers or Cummings could easily find themselves recalled after a prolific, headline-making few months.

Moore and Mubama put the England Under 21s 2-0 up within half an hour at the home of Bristol City.

Aladji Bamba then one of three French players to be subbed on 64 minutes.

The Newcastle United midfielder watched on from the sidelines as his teammates staged a comeback, scoring in the 80th and 85th minutes.

However, in the 89th minute it was Arsenal’s Max Dowman who got the winning goal in this Under 21s friendly.

Elsewhere, a remarkable night in Berlin as Jurgen Klopp saw his Germany side play out their sixth match under his leadership.

His reign had started in dismal fashion with defeat to Greece and a draw with the Netherlands in their opening two Nations League group games.

Jurgen Klopp then made a number of changes which included bringing in Malick Thiaw and in their next three games, Germany picked up seven points from a possible nine and only conceded one goal.

Having played the full match in the win over Serbia on Friday, the Newcastle United defender was rested last night in Berlin.

Germany pulling off a stunning 5-0 victory over the Netherlands as they somehow came back from what looked an impossible position to win their Nations League group.

Serbia ended the group without a single point but the other three nations all with 11 points, Jurgen Klopp and his players just edging out the Netherlands and Greece.

Earlier on Monday, another full match and another international victory for Newcastle United’s Ousmane Diabaté, the exciting midfield prospect played the full match as the 19-year-old helped Guinea to a 3-1 AFCON qualifying group win over Eritrea.

Ousmane Diabaté was still only 18 when signing for Newcastle United this summer but already a full international for Guinea. He was also a first choice regular for his club side in the Turkish top tier, United agreeing Diabaté could stay with Gençlerbirliği this season in order to continue to get regular first team football at club level.

Francesco Camarda got on target for Italy’s U21 side last night as they beat France by two goals to one, bagging the opener.

It has been a tough season for Camarda so far. After a pre-season and summer that seemed to promise consistent playing time this season, the youngster has only racked up 119 minutes on the pitch between Serie A and the Europa League.

According to recent reports, no goals have been scored either, which is obviously never ideal for a striker looking to grow. A loan move appears to be on the cards, but the January window isn’t for another month and a half, so a confidence boost cannot come swiftly enough. Luckily, he got one last night.

Italy U21 played a friendly against France in Laval last night and Camarda managed to get the opener in the game. After picking up a good position, the striker veered off into the centre and found the open space in France’s defence.

It has been revealed that camarda received the ball from Matteo Dagasso and while it looked for a split second like the pass was overhit, he got on the end of it and found the back of the net. Once again, as we have seen with Milan this season too, his movement was crucial in creating the chance.

Let’s see what happens in the coming weeks, but perhaps he can get some more chances by Amorim and finally score his first goal with the red and black shirt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The value of international friendlies has always seemed questionable mid season: During a challenging domestic schedule the disruption of thousands of miles of travel, different coaching regimes and playing styles can easily prove disruptive: Let alone the risk of injuries to jaded players.

West Ham United have their fair share of absentees on international duty right now, which Scott Parker must be rueing as he tries to rebuild the playing style of the squad he has inherited from his predecessor.

However there’s an upside to  those international fixtures if it allows squad members to improve their game and their confidence – and several of the Hammers’ squad will come back to their club in far better spirits than they left.

As we covered yesterday Mads Hermansen’s headline winning performance to keep out Portugal can only have done him good.

International debut for Hammers youngster Mohamadou Kanté.

Mohamadou Kanté must be made up at making his international debut for Mali – on the winning side in his first time wearing the national shirt means the midfield man will come back with a little more of a swagger than he left with, whilst news of Joel Piroe’s brace on international duty for Suriname will have been similarly well received at Rush Green.

With Castellanos and Pablo misfiring so badly, much is expected of the on-loan Leeds man and for Piroe to grab two goals in his national side’s 4-0 victory over Eswatini (formerly Swaziland, for anyone else who wondered) can only be a confidence boost for West Ham’s number nine ahead of the resumption of the Championship at the weekend.

#14629. Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts

Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 45 min read (8944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~45 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, a Lancet Commission proposed distinguishing clinical obesity, defined by adiposity-related organ dysfunction, from preclinical obesity, defined by excess adiposity with preserved function, and recommended using anthropometric measures beyond body mass index (BMI) to confirm obesity status1.
  • Medical diagnoses typically define disease on the basis of objective signs of organ dysfunction2 (see https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/diagnosis).
  • The absence of a clinically grounded definition has impeded recognition of obesity as a distinct disease, contributing to gaps in care, inconsistent prevention, misallocated resources and persistent stigma6,7.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, a Lancet Commission proposed distinguishing clinical obesity, defined by adiposity-related organ dysfunction, from preclinical obesity, defined by excess adiposity with preserved function, and recommended using anthropometric measures beyond body mass index (BMI) to confirm obesity status1. Here we report the comparative performance of this framework versus conventional BMI-based classification using prevalence, incidence and mortality data from 844,108 adults across four cohorts in China, the UK, the USA and Spain. Complementing BMI with waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio data demonstrated that BMI alone overestimated obesity in 1.2–3.1% and underestimated it in 5.2–8.6% of participants across cohorts. The combined anthropometric definition increased overall obesity prevalence by 3.3–7.4% relative to BMI-based classification. Clinical obesity accounted for 22.7–31.3% of total obesity, with an overall population prevalence of 5.6–10.9%. A large proportion of individuals (between 77.4% and 91.3%) with preclinical obesity at baseline showed no progression to clinical obesity over 10 years. Increased mortality risk was associated with the combined anthropometric definition of obesity, but not with BMI-only obesity. Clinical obesity was associated with substantially higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.69, 95% confidence interval 1.64–1.73), whereas preclinical obesity conferred only modest risk (1.19, 1.14–1.24). These findings support the global adoption of the Lancet Commission diagnostic framework to improve obesity care and policy.

Medical diagnoses typically define disease on the basis of objective signs of organ dysfunction2 (see https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/diagnosis). By contrast, the health impact of obesity has historically been assessed using body mass index (BMI)—a proxy for body size—alongside obesity-related comorbidities3,4,5. This approach provides an aggregate measure of ill health rather than a disease-specific diagnosis.

The absence of a clinically grounded definition has impeded recognition of obesity as a distinct disease, contributing to gaps in care, inconsistent prevention, misallocated resources and persistent stigma6,7.

To address this, in 2025, a Lancet Commission from The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology proposed a upcoming diagnostic framework that distinguishes between two categories of obesity: clinical obesity, defined by excess adiposity impairing organ function or daily activities; and preclinical obesity, characterized by increased adiposity and increased health risks but with preserved organ and whole-body function1. The framework also recommends supplementing BMI with other anthropometric measures, such as waist circumference (WC), waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) or fat quantification with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, when available, to improve the detection of excess adiposity. Although consistent conceptually with diagnostic principles in medicine, the clinical implications of this framework remain uncertain. It is unknown how substantially the recommended use of additional anthropometric measures changes the classification of obesity compared with BMI alone, or whether the distinction between clinical and preclinical obesity captures meaningfully different health states. The natural history of preclinical obesity is also poorly characterized, including the extent to which it remains stable or progresses to clinical obesity over time. More broadly, whether these classifications show consistent associations with prognosis across populations and healthcare settings has yet to be established. We examined these questions using data from 844,108 adults from four large cohorts in China, the UK, the USA and Spain, aiming to evaluate the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic framework in terms of obesity classification, the distribution and longitudinal course of clinical and preclinical obesity and their associations with mortality.

To assess whether incorporating other anthropometric measures (WC and WHtR) improves obesity detection beyond the use of BMI alone, we analysed data from four cohorts: the Kailuan Study (China, n = 137,795), the UK Biobank (UKB, n = 436,203), the All of Us Research Program (AoU; USA, n = 218,841) and the SIDIAP database (Spain, n = 51,269). The characteristics of the study populations are shown in Supplementary Table 1, selection of study participants from each cohort is shown in Supplementary Figs. 1–4 and the details of study design of each cohort are presented in the Methods and Supplementary Methods. Following the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic criteria1, obesity confirmation required any of the following three components: (1) BMI ≥ 40.0 kg m−2; (2) BMI ≥ 30.0 kg m−2 (≥28.0 kg m−2 for Chinese individuals) plus elevated WC or elevated WHtR; or (3) BMI 25.0–29.9 kg m−2 (24.0–27.9 kg m−2 for Chinese individuals) plus both elevated WC and elevated WHtR. Elevated WC was defined as ≥102 cm for male and ≥88 cm for female individuals (≥90/85 cm (male/female) for Chinese individuals)8,9, and WHtR thresholds varied by ethnicity (non-Hispanic white: male/female ≥0.57/0.58; non-Hispanic Black: ≥0.55/0.57; Hispanic: ≥0.57/0.59; Asian: ≥0.56/0.59; others: ≥0.50)10.

Classification based on BMI alone resulted in both over- and under-identification of obesity across all four cohorts (Fig. 1 and Extended Data Table 1). The proportions classified as obese by BMI but without elevated WC or WHtR were 3.1% in the Kailuan Study, 1.9% in the UKB, 1.9% in the AoU and 1.2% in the SIDIAP, whereas 6.6%, 5.2%, 7.5% and 8.6%, respectively, of individuals with BMI-defined overweight met both WC and WHtR criteria for obesity-level adiposity. With the Lancet Commission’s recommended multi-criteria definition, hereafter referred to as the combined anthropometric definition of obesity (CAD-obesity), overall obesity prevalence increased from 17.8% to 21.3% in the Kailuan Study, 24.0% to 27.3% in the UKB, 42.5% to 48.1% in the AoU and 18.7% to 26.1% in the SIDIAP. Overall, CAD-obesity yielded a modest net increase in obesity prevalence of 3.5% in China, 3.3% in the UK, 5.6% in the USA and 7.4% in Spain.

Definitions of BMI-based obesity, WC-based obesity, WHtR-based obesity and CAD-obesity are provided in the Methods. The analyses included 137,795 participants from the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants from the UK Biobank, 218,841 participants from the All of Us (AoU) Research Program and 51,269 participants from the SIDIAP database. Prevalence estimates are presented as percentages. a, Prevalence of obesity defined separately by BMI, WC and WHtR. b, Reclassification of obesity status across BMI-defined categories after applying CAD-obesity criteria. Colours indicate the corresponding reclassification categories as defined in the figure.

It has been revealed that clinical obesity was defined as CAD-obesity accompanied by at least one of the 18 adult diagnostic criteria specified by the Lancet Commission. These criteria represent obesity-related organ dysfunction or functional impairment across several systems, including cardiovascular (for example, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, thromboembolic disease and hypertension), respiratory (obstructive sleep apnoea and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), metabolic (combined dysglycaemia and dyslipidaemia), hepatic (MASLD with fibrosis), renal (chronic kidney disease), neurological (intracranial hypertension), musculoskeletal (hip or knee osteoarthritis), reproductive (infertility), urological (urinary incontinence) and lymphatic dysfunctions, together with limitations in daily activities. Criteria for clinical obesity were operationalized using predefined clinical, laboratory, imaging or diagnostic criteria adapted to the variables available in each cohort. Detailed definitions and cohort-specific assessment methods are provided in the Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Table 2.

Industry observers note that however, not all organ dysfunction that coexists with CAD-obesity can be assumed to be attributable to obesity. We therefore applied an attributable fraction (AF) approach to provide a population-level estimate of attribution and to adjust subsequent estimates accordingly11. The AF was calculated as: \({\rm{AF}}=\frac{{\rm{HR}}-1}{{\rm{HR}}}\), where HR denotes the hazard ratio for the association between CAD-obesity and risk of incident organ dysfunction with adjustment for relevant confounders using Cox proportional hazards models. The cohort-specific HRs used to derive the AF estimates were 1.62 (95% confidence interval (CI), 1.58–1.66) in the Kailuan Study, 1.68 (1.64–1.72) in the UKB, 1.67 (1.61–1.73) in the AoU and 2.07 (1.97–2.18) in the SIDIAP (Extended Data Table 2), corresponding to AF values of 0.383, 0.405, 0.401 and 0.517, respectively.

Industry observers note that because the distinction between clinical and preclinical obesity depends on the presence of organ dysfunction among individuals with CAD-obesity, we first quantified the observed crude prevalence of organ dysfunction and then applied the cohort-specific AF estimates to account for the proportion plausibly attributable to obesity at the population level. The crude prevalence of organ dysfunction among people with CAD-obesity ranged from 56.7% in the AoU to 75.3% in the UKB (Fig. 2; Extended Data Table 3). AF-adjusted clinical obesity accounted for 26.3% (95% CI: 25.2–27.3) of total obesity in the Kailuan Study, 30.5% (29.4–31.6) in the UKB, 22.7% (21.5–24.0) in the AoU, and 31.3% (30.9–31.8) in the SIDIAP (Fig. 2; Extended Data Table 3). Accordingly, the proportion of individuals with CAD-obesity but without any detectable organ dysfunction—representing the minimum estimate of preclinical obesity—ranged from 24.7% in the UKB to 43.3% in the AoU, and the maximum estimate of preclinical obesity (1 minus the AF-adjusted prevalence of clinical obesity) ranged from 68.7% in the SIDIAP to 77.3% in the AoU (Extended Data Table 3).

Definitions of CAD-obesity, preclinical obesity and clinical obesity are provided in the Methods. The analyses included 137,795 participants from the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants from the UK Biobank, 218,841 participants from the All of Us Research Program and 51,269 participants from the SIDIAP database. Grey segments represent individuals without CAD-obesity. Orange segments represent the estimated AF-adjusted prevalence component of clinical obesity, corresponding to CAD-obesity with organ dysfunction statistically attributable to CAD-obesity at the population level. Green segments represent individuals with CAD-obesity but without evidence of organ dysfunction. Segments with a colour gradient represent the estimated non-attributable prevalence component among participants with CAD-obesity and organ dysfunction after application of the AF adjustment. Together, the green and gradient segments represent the estimated AF-adjusted prevalence of preclinical obesity.

The overall prevalence of AF-adjusted clinical obesity in the full population was 5.6% (95% CI: 5.4–5.8) in the Kailuan Study, 8.3% (8.0–8.6) in the UKB, 10.9% (10.4–11.5) in the AoU and 8.2% (8.1–8.3) in the SIDIAP (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Table 3).

Recent findings suggest that sensitivity analyses restricting to the nine organ dysfunction indicators available across all datasets yielded results that were highly consistent with the primary analyses. Prevalence estimates changed minimally under the restricted definition, indicating that additional cohort-specific indicators contributed little to classification (Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Indicators that were not universally available were individually rare, and most participants presenting them also had at least one of the nine common indicators, supporting the robustness and comparability of the classification across cohorts (Supplementary Table 5).

To assess the progression from preclinical to clinical obesity, we performed an analysis among individuals with CAD-obesity but without any organ dysfunction at baseline. The AF-adjusted 10-year incidence of clinical obesity was 21.2% in the Kailuan Study, 8.7% in the UKB and 22.6% in the SIDIAP; because of a shorter follow-up in the AoU cohort, only an AF-adjusted 4-year incidence was calculated and an incidence of 8.5% was found (Fig. 3). Thus, approximately 70–90% of individuals with preclinical obesity remained stable over a decade. The incidence rates were similar between male and female individuals (Supplementary Fig. 5), and sensitivity analysis restricting to the nine organ dysfunction indicators yielded similar results (Kailuan Study: 21.4%; UK Biobank: 8.8%).

The analyses included 8,009 participants from the Kailuan Study, 29,338 participants from the UK Biobank, 54,535 participants from the All of Us Research Program and 5,273 participants from the SIDIAP database, all of whom had preclinical obesity at baseline. Solid lines represent the estimated cumulative incidence of clinical obesity, calculated by applying AF-based estimates to the observed incidence of organ dysfunction among individuals with preclinical obesity. Dashed lines represent the observed cumulative incidence of incident organ dysfunction. Shaded areas represent the corresponding 95% CIs. Cumulative incidence curves were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods and were generated from baseline until incident organ dysfunction, death or the end of follow-up, whichever occurred first. AF estimates were calculated from HRs derived using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for cohort-specific covariates, as described in the Supplementary Methods.

Sources indicate that cox proportional hazards models were used to assess associations of BMI-based obesity and CAD-obesity with all-cause mortality, adjusting for sociodemographic covariates. The AoU cohort was excluded because of limited follow-up. Median follow-up was 15.3 years in the Kailuan Study (17,642 deaths), 13.8 years in the UKB (31,812 deaths) and 11.2 years in the SIDIAP (2,338 deaths).

In a recent development, compared with individuals with no overweight or obesity, participants with BMI-defined overweight or obesity but without CAD-obesity had a lower all-cause mortality risk (pooled HR 0.88 [95% CI: 0.86–0.90] and 0.93 [0.86–0.99], respectively). By contrast, individuals with CAD-obesity, regardless of whether their BMI was in the overweight or obese range, had a significantly higher, albeit modest, mortality risk (pooled HR 1.06 [1.03–1.10] and 1.07 [1.05–1.10], respectively; Fig. 4a and Extended Data Table 4).

Industry observers note that the analyses included 137,792 participants from the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants from the UK Biobank and 51,269 participants from the SIDIAP database. Each panel presents Kaplan–Meier survival curves and adjusted HRs with 95% CIs for all-cause mortality, with cohort-specific survival curves shown on the left and pooled HR estimates from Cox proportional hazards models shown on the right. Solid lines in Kaplan–Meier plots represent survival probability estimates for each obesity classification group, with colours indicating the categories defined in each panel. Shaded areas around survival curves indicate 95% CIs. In forest plots, points represent HR point estimates and horizontal lines represent corresponding 95% CIs. The x axes of the forest plots are presented on a logarithmic scale. Cox proportional hazards models were adjusted for cohort-specific covariates as specified in the Supplementary Methods, and pooled HR estimates were obtained using fixed-effects models. All statistical tests were two-sided, and no adjustment for multiple comparisons was performed. a, Mortality risk according to BMI-based overweight or obesity and CAD-obesity status. Colours indicate BMI-based categories combined with CAD-obesity status: no overweight or obesity; overweight BMI without CAD-obesity; BMI-based obesity without CAD-obesity; overweight BMI with CAD-obesity; and BMI-based obesity with CAD-obesity. b, Mortality risk according to obesity stage defined by CAD-obesity and organ dysfunction, including preclinical and clinical obesity. Colours indicate four groups: no CAD-obesity and no organ dysfunction; no CAD-obesity with organ dysfunction; CAD-obesity without organ dysfunction (preclinical obesity); and CAD-obesity with organ dysfunction (clinical obesity).

Further cause-specific mortality analyses were done in the UK Biobank (the only cohort with available cause-specific mortality data), including cardiovascular mortality, obesity-related cancer mortality and their combination (Supplementary Table 6). After multivariable adjustment, BMI-defined overweight or obesity without CAD-obesity was not associated with increased risks of these cause-specific mortality outcomes. By contrast, CAD-obesity was associated with higher risks, including among individuals in the BMI-defined overweight range.

Sources indicate that in further sensitivity analyses, exclusion of deaths occurring within the first 5 years of follow-up did not materially alter the associations, arguing against reverse causation as a major explanation for the findings (Supplementary Table 7). The proportion of missingness was low across all cohorts, with no variable exceeding 20% (Supplementary Table 8), and a sensitivity analysis restricted to participants without missing variables also yielded robust results (Supplementary Table 9). Stratified analyses by smoking status confirmed that smoking was a strong effect modifier; however, among never-smokers, CAD-obesity remained consistently associated with higher mortality risk, whereas BMI-defined overweight and obesity in the absence of CAD-obesity revealed no or modest mortality risk after multivariable adjustment (Supplementary Table 10).

We evaluated the association between clinical obesity and mortality risk. Participants were first categorized into four baseline groups: (1) no CAD-obesity and no organ dysfunction (reference group); (2) no CAD-obesity with organ dysfunction; (3) CAD-obesity without organ dysfunction (preclinical obesity); and (4) CAD-obesity with organ dysfunction (clinical obesity). Clinical obesity was associated with a substantially higher mortality risk (pooled HR, 1.69; 95% CI, 1.64–1.73), whereas preclinical obesity demonstrated a modest association (pooled HR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.14–1.24; Fig. 4b and Extended Data Table 5). Cohort-specific estimates were directionally consistent.

Sensitivity analyses by excluding deaths occurring within the first 2 or 5 years of follow-up or by incorporating waist-to-hip ratio into the diagnostic indicators did not materially alter the associations (Extended Data Table 6). The association between clinical obesity and mortality was stronger in female individuals and in those aged younger than 60 years (P < 0.001 for interactions; Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 11). In the age-stratified analysis, sensitivity analyses by further excluding deaths occurring within the first 5 years or restricting participants without missing variables yielded similar results to those of the primary analysis (Supplementary Tables 12 and 13), providing further reassurance against reverse causation and selection biases.

Industry observers note that to disentangle the relative contributions of BMI-defined obesity, CAD-obesity and organ dysfunction to mortality risk, participants were further classified into eight groups according to the presence or absence of each component. In groups defined by organ dysfunction and CAD-obesity, BMI-defined obesity conferred little additional risk, when compared with the BMI-defined non-obese status. On the other hand, CAD-obesity highlighted a consistently higher mortality risk, and the highest mortality risks were observed among participants with both CAD-obesity and organ dysfunction (that is, clinical obesity) (Extended Data Table 7).

Separate cause-specific mortality analyses of clinical and preclinical obesity in the UK Biobank dataset indicated that clinical obesity was consistently associated with substantially higher risks, with effect sizes generally stronger than those observed for all-cause mortality, whereas preclinical obesity showed elevated but consistently lower risks (Supplementary Table 14).

We performed further complementary analyses to examine the appropriateness of the ethnicity-specific WHtR thresholds used to confirm obesity status. First, the relationship between BMI and WHtR was broadly consistent across cohorts (Pearson r ≥ 0.64; Extended Data Fig. 2). On the basis of fitted linear regression models, the conventional WHtR cut-off of 0.50 corresponded approximately to the BMI-defined overweight threshold, whereas WHtR values corresponding to the BMI-defined obesity threshold were generally higher than 0.55 (from 0.55 to 0.60 across the four cohorts).

Mortality analyses showed a similar pattern. Restricted cubic spline models indicated that mortality risk began to increase at WHtR values around 0.55 (Extended Data Fig. 3). Consistently, participants with a WHtR between 0.50 and the ethnicity-specific thresholds had no excess mortality risk (pooled HR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.97–1.02), whereas those with a WHtR above the ethnicity-specific threshold had a higher risk (pooled HR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.18–1.24; Supplementary Table 15).

It has been revealed that using 0.50 instead of the ethnicity-specific thresholds substantially increased the proportion of participants defined as having obesity by meeting the WHtR criterion across all four cohorts (Kailuan, 59.2% versus 18.3%; UKB, 66.7% versus 27.2%; AoU, 74.3% versus 48.8%; SIDIAP, 71.1% versus 33.3%). When these thresholds were incorporated into the definition of confirmed obesity, the same risk pattern was observed: participants classified only by the 0.50 threshold indicated no excess mortality (pooled HR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.96–1.03), whereas those meeting the ethnicity-specific thresholds had a higher mortality risk (pooled HR, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.18–1.22; Supplementary Table 16).

To our knowledge, this is the first large-scale, multinational study to comprehensively evaluate the Lancet Commission diagnostic framework1 against the widely used BMI-based classification. Previous studies have examined individual components of the framework—such as expanded anthropometric criteria or prevalence estimates of clinical obesity—but have lacked integrated assessment or longitudinal follow-up12,13,14,15,16. This study evaluated several interrelated elements of the new diagnostic framework: the implications of using combined anthropometric criteria to confirm obesity; their effects on prevalence and risk stratification compared with BMI alone; the importance of selecting appropriate anthropometric cut-offs; and the prognostic implications of distinguishing clinical from preclinical obesity.

It has been revealed that with regard to anthropometric classification, our findings show that BMI alone both over- and under-identifies obesity and does not reliably distinguish individuals who have an increased mortality risk. These results support the Commission framework’s use of complementary anthropometric measures alongside BMI to improve obesity classification and risk stratification. Although WC and WHtR are, like BMI, indirect measures of adiposity, increased values for these measures are (for anatomical and physiological reasons) more likely to reflect fat-mass expansion, whereas a higher BMI might also reflect greater lean mass. Their correlation with direct body-composition measurements10 supports their use as a pragmatic means of detecting excess adiposity where direct measurement is impractical. Future studies should determine whether direct measurement of fat adds meaningful precision and could ultimately replace combined anthropometry if reliable bedside technologies become widely available.

We observed substantial discordance between BMI-based classification and CAD-obesity, with BMI overestimating obesity in 1.2–3.1% and underestimating it in 5.2–8.6% of participants across cohorts. When considered against national obesity estimates from the 2025 World Obesity Atlas17, these proportions suggest that BMI misclassification affects tens of millions of individuals in countries with large populations, underscoring the potential public-health implications of seemingly modest differences in classification.

In a recent development, however, the effects of using a combined anthropometric definition of obesity depend, crucially, on how the Commission’s recommendations are operationalized. Unlike our findings, previous studies in US cohorts reported that applying the Lancet Commission framework substantially increased overall obesity prevalence12,13,14,15,16. These discrepancies mainly reflect methodological differences, particularly the choice of anthropometric cut-offs and incomplete adherence to the framework’s recommendations. In one study14, higher prevalence estimates were driven by the use of a single low WHtR cut-off of 0.50 across populations, potentially classifying individuals with milder increases in adiposity and associated risk as having obesity. Another study16 reported an overall obesity prevalence of 60% in the AoU cohort, compared with 48.1% in our analysis. In addition to using a single WHtR cut-off of 0.50, the study applied the cut-off across the full BMI range, including individuals with a normal BMI. This approach diverges from the Commission’s recommendation that anthropometric confirmation be used mainly in individuals with BMI values below—but near —the BMI obesity threshold1. Applying anthropometric criteria outside this context risks classifying individuals with normal body weight and localized abdominal adiposity—such as those with lipodystrophy or related conditions, which are biologically and clinically distinct—as having obesity. For this reason, the Commission retained BMI as the initial screening tool1, and we limited the assessment of obesity to participants within the conventional BMI-defined overweight and obesity ranges.

Industry observers note that in closer alignment with the Commission’s guidance, we applied obesity-level, ethnicity-specific thresholds for WC and WHtR. In our data, the conventional WHtR cut-off of 0.50 corresponded approximately to the BMI-defined overweight threshold, whereas WHtR values corresponding to the BMI-defined obesity threshold and increasing mortality risk were generally observed around or above 0.55. This convergence between anthropometric and mortality analyses supports the use of higher WHtR thresholds for obesity classification and is consistent with the previously proposed cut-off of 0.55–0.59 (ref. 10). Further prospective evaluation will be required to refine population-specific thresholds.

Industry observers note that the application of obesity-level thresholds for WC and WHtR further illustrates the limitations of BMI-based classification. Although these measures remain indirect proxies of body fat, the reclassified groups had distinct mortality profiles, showing that conventional BMI categories encompass individuals with heterogeneous risk and that additional measures provide clinically relevant stratification beyond BMI alone. This is particularly consequential for the overweight category. The Lancet Commission framework intentionally does not retain overweight as a separate intermediate-risk category; instead, it extends the definition of obesity to individuals with a BMI classified as overweight who meet additional anthropometric criteria indicating obesity-level adiposity. Our data support this approach: individuals with a BMI in the overweight range who met CAD-obesity criteria had a mortality risk comparable with that of individuals with a BMI in the obesity range who also met CAD-obesity criteria. By contrast, those with a BMI classified as overweight who did not meet CAD-obesity criteria had no excess risk and, in several analyses, had a lower risk than did individuals with a normal BMI. The CAD-obesity criteria therefore identify adiposity-related risk that would otherwise remain obscured within the conventional overweight range.

The implications are substantial. An estimated 1.5 billion adults worldwide are classified as overweight by BMI17, yet our findings indicate that individuals in this population should not all be regarded as being at increased risk. Our data suggest that combining BMI with WC and appropriately calibrated WHtR cut-offs, such as those evaluated here, can identify higher-risk individuals without substantially increasing overall obesity prevalence. This selective reclassification provides a clinically meaningful basis to inform individual care, health policy and resource allocation.

Anthropometric confirmation improves the identification of mortality risk associated with excess adiposity. However, because clinical obesity denotes an active disease state, its diagnosis requires a further step: establishing the presence of organ dysfunction that can plausibly be attributed to that adiposity. This requirement reflects a fundamental principle of disease definition: because similar alterations in organ function can arise from different disease processes, causality cannot be inferred from coexistence alone. For example, not all joint inflammation is caused by rheumatoid arthritis, nor is all heart failure attributable to the same underlying heart disease. In clinical practice, differential diagnosis addresses this uncertainty by considering alternative causes and, where possible, excluding them; it is therefore essential to diagnostic specificity. For this reason, organ dysfunction coexisting with obesity cannot automatically be considered obesity-related; doing so could overattribute dysfunction to obesity and substantially inflate estimates of clinical-obesity prevalence and incidence. Most previous applications of the framework classified all coexisting organ dysfunction as obesity-related without accounting for alternative causes13,14,15,16, and might therefore have overestimated the prevalence of clinical obesity.

Sources indicate that to mitigate this problem, we applied the AF method at the population level to estimate the proportion of organ dysfunction that is statistically attributable to CAD-obesity, and adjusted the prevalence and incidence estimates accordingly. Although this adjustment cannot establish causality in individual participants, it mitigates the risk of attributing organ dysfunction to obesity when other causes could be responsible, thereby reducing systematic overattribution and improving population-level estimates of the prevalence and incidence of clinical obesity. Notably, an earlier US study12 using a different adjustment approach estimated the clinical-obesity prevalence as 9.7%, close to the 10.9% that was observed in the AoU cohort after AF adjustment. This concordance between studies using different population-level methods to account for plausible attribution provides some reassurance about the robustness of our estimates.

It has been revealed that our longitudinal and mortality analyses provide evidence supporting the distinction between clinical and preclinical obesity. Despite variation across cohorts, 70–90% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity over 10 years. Clinical obesity was also associated with substantially higher all-cause and obesity-related mortality, whereas preclinical obesity indicated only a modest excess mortality risk. The observed patterns of progression and differences in mortality risk show that these health states differ not only in their defining clinical characteristics but also in their prognostic implications. The distinct clinical and prognostic profiles of clinical and preclinical obesity provide a foundation for personalized, proportionate care. Preclinical obesity warrants a mostly preventive approach aimed at reducing future risk, with the nature and intensity of intervention guided by the individual’s risk of progression and the presence of relevant comorbidities. By contrast, established functional impairment and higher mortality risk in clinical obesity justify greater urgency and, where appropriate, more intensive treatment and prioritized access. The distinction can therefore guide the purpose, timing and intensity of individual care and support evidence-based decisions on treatment prioritization, coverage and resource allocation.

Recent findings suggest that notably, using this distinction to guide proportionate care does not imply withholding treatment from people with preclinical obesity. One criticism of the Lancet Commission framework is that distinguishing preclinical from clinical obesity could encourage ‘watchful waiting’ or restrict access to treatment18,19,20. However, this concern seems to conflate diagnostic classification with treatment eligibility. Like any diagnosis, the distinction between clinical and preclinical obesity provides a snapshot of an individual’s current health status; it does not prescribe inaction or determine eligibility for treatment by itself. Analogous distinctions—such as those between prediabetes and diabetes or adenomatous polyps and carcinoma—guide the purpose, urgency and intensity of intervention without precluding care for prediabetes or adenomatous polyps21. Accordingly, preclinical obesity might warrant active preventive treatment, including lifestyle, pharmacological or, in selected cases, surgical interventions, depending on progression risk and comorbidities that could benefit from weight reduction. Treatment decisions should therefore be informed by diagnosis but not reduced to diagnostic category alone.

Recent findings suggest that several limitations should be acknowledged. The retrospective design of our study and its reliance on electronic health record (EHR) data could limit diagnostic precision and introduce inter-cohort variability. Organ dysfunction was identified using administrative codes rather than standardized clinical assessments, and not all 18 dysfunction indicators were available in every cohort, potentially leading to the underestimation or misclassification of specific organ disease subtypes. This limitation is highlighted by the Kailuan cohort, in which the higher observed incidence of clinical obesity might reflect more frequent (biennial) clinical evaluations. However, sensitivity analyses highlighted that the additional indicators contributed minimally to classification, supporting the conclusion that differences in the number of available organ-dysfunction indicators are unlikely to be a major driver of the inter-cohort variability observed in the primary analyses. Finally, the AF method cannot determine attribution at the individual level, and future prospective studies using clinically adjudicated diagnoses of clinical and preclinical obesity will be essential to refine estimates of disease burden and progression. Nonetheless, the consistency of findings across geographically and demographically diverse cohorts strengthens the robustness, generalizability and clinical relevance of the proposed diagnostic framework.

Industry observers note that in summary, BMI alone misclassifies obesity in a substantial proportion of individuals, both overestimating and underestimating the clinical relevance of excess adiposity, and does not meaningfully discriminate higher mortality risk. Integrating other anthropometric measures (such as WHtR and WC) and clinical criteria reflecting organ function into a multi-criteria framework improves obesity detection and aligns diagnosis more closely with true disease status. Clinical and preclinical obesity represent distinct and prevalent subgroups, with markedly different mortality risks. This study demonstrates the clinical utility and prognostic importance of distinguishing between clinical and preclinical obesity, and supports the global applicability of this classification scheme for guiding care and informing health policy.

This population-based multinational study analysed data from four large and well-characterized adult cohorts: the Kailuan Study (China), the UK Biobank (UKB; UK), the All of Us Research Program (AoU; USA), and the Information System for the Development of Research in Primary Care (SIDIAP, Spain). The Kailuan Study is an ongoing prospective cohort initiated between 2006 and 2007 among more than 100,000 employees of the Kailuan Group, with biennial follow-up examinations thereafter22. The UK Biobank enrolled around 500,000 individuals aged 37–73 years from 2006 to 2010 with questionnaires, physical examinations and biomarker assessments23. The All of Us Research Program is a US precision-medicine initiative aimed at building a diverse biomedical database to study the biological, clinical, social and environmental determinants of health24. The SIDIAP database includes pseudonymized EHRs from more than eight million individuals in Catalonia since 2006, with approximately 75% of the regional population represented25.

It has been revealed that the Kailuan Study was approved by the ethics committee of the Kailuan Medical Group. The UK Biobank received ethical approval from the North West Multi-Centre Research Ethics Committee. The All of Us Research Program is overseen by the All of Us institutional review board. The SIDIAP analysis was approved by the IDIAP Jordi Gol ethics committee (20/204-P). All studies followed the Declaration of Helsinki, and all participants gave their written informed consent. No additional ethical approval was required for the current study because no new data were collected and all analyses were performed using previously collected data.

Participants aged 18–74 years who were free from stroke, myocardial infarction and cancer at baseline and for whom anthropometric (BMI, WC and WHtR) and organ-dysfunction data were available were included. The final numbers included in the prevalence estimates were 137,795 from the Kailuan Study, 436,203 from the UKB, 218,841 from the AoU and 51,269 from the SIDIAP. The progression from preclinical obesity to clinical obesity was estimated among those with CAD-confirmed obesity but without any organ dysfunction, and the sample size was 8,009, 29,338, 54,535 and 5,273, respectively. For the mortality analysis, the AoU study was excluded owing to its relatively short follow-up duration; for the other three cohorts, the sample size was generally the same as that in the prevalence analysis, except for the Kailuan Study, in which three participants without valid mortality data were further excluded. Details of the study design for each cohort can be found in the Supplementary Methods, and the selection of study participants is in Supplementary Figs. 1–4.

According to recent reports, following criteria from the Lancet Commission1, clinical obesity was defined as excess adiposity plus at least one sign of obesity-induced organ dysfunction. Preclinical obesity was defined as excess adiposity without such dysfunction.

Industry observers note that excess adiposity was defined by any of the following criteria, to be consistent with the proposed framework: (1) BMI ≥ 40 kg m−2; (2) BMI ≥ 30 kg m−2 (≥28 for Chinese individuals) plus elevated WC or WHtR; or (3) BMI 25–30 kg m−2 (24–28 for Chinese individuals) plus both elevated WC and WHtR. The thresholds for population-specific WC-defined adiposity are ≥102 cm for male and ≥88 cm for female individuals in the Western population, and ≥90 cm for male and ≥85 cm for female individuals in the Chinese population8,9. The thresholds for race- and sex-specific WHtR-defined adiposity are 0.57 (male) and 0.58 (female) for non-Hispanic white individuals; 0.55 (male) and 0.57 (female) for non-Hispanic Black individuals; 0.57 (male) and 0.59 (female) for Hispanic individuals; 0.56 (male) and 0.59 (female) for Asian individuals; and 0.50 for others10. To illustrate that the commonly used WHtR cut-off of 0.50 (ref. 26) is not an appropriate measure for central obesity, the bivariate scatter plots between BMI and WHtR were generated with fitted linear regression lines. The optimal cut-off values for WHtR that correspond to established BMI thresholds of obesity (28 kg m−2 for Chinese individuals and 30 for others) were derived from the linear regression lines given the very high Pearson correlation coefficients in the four cohorts (r ≥ 0.64).

Organ dysfunction was defined as the presence of at least one of 18 clinical indicators listed in the Commission report. Notably, in line with the Commission’s recommendations, the metabolic cluster criterion for clinical obesity (hyperglycaemia together with low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and high triglycerides) was considered to be met only when diabetes and dyslipidaemia occurred together, and not when either condition occurred alone. Data availability about organ dysfunction ranged from 9 (SIDIAP) to 18 (UKB) indicators. Case ascertainment was based on medical records, self-reports and health assessments (Supplementary Table 2).

Socio-demographic and lifestyle data were collected for each cohort; details can be found in the Supplementary Methods.

Organ dysfunction and death events were identified through self-reports, clinical exams, medical records and provincial death certificates in the Kailuan Study. In the UKB, events were ascertained through linkages with hospital records and death registries. Incident organ dysfunctions were obtained through EHRs in the AoU study, with measurements recorded at different time points and clinic visits. Outcomes in the SIDIAP were identified through linkage to primary care and hospital EHRs.

Given the challenges in establishing causality between obesity and coexisting organ dysfunction at the individual level, we applied the AF approach at the population level to quantify the proportion of organ dysfunction cases attributable to obesity among individuals with obesity11. The AF was calculated as: \({\rm{AF}}=\frac{{\rm{HR}}-1}{{\rm{HR}}}\), where HR denotes the hazard ratio for the association between obesity and risk of incident organ dysfunction with adjustment for relevant confounders using Cox proportional hazards models. Details are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

It has been revealed that descriptive statistics were reported as mean (s.d.), median (interquartile range) or percentages, as appropriate. Multiple imputations using chained equations (linear and logistic regression) were used to impute the missing data (mice package in R, v.3.19.0). Prevalence estimates and 95% CIs were calculated using the epi.conf function from the epiR package in R (v.2.0.95). To quantify the misclassification of obesity by BMI alone, we estimated the prevalence of abdominal obesity (based on WC and/or WHtR) in each BMI category. We further estimated the prevalence of clinical obesity among people with obesity, as well as among the total population, with adjustment using the AF method. The AF-adjusted prevalence of clinical obesity was estimated by multiplying the crude prevalence of clinical obesity and the corresponding AF values in each cohort. The unadjusted prevalence (that is, the observed prevalence) was considered as the maximum of the prevalence of clinical obesity.

According to recent reports, using longitudinal data from all four cohorts, we estimated the cumulative incidence of incident organ dysfunction among individuals with preclinical obesity. Follow-up time was calculated from baseline until the first occurrence of incident organ dysfunction, death or end of follow-up. Cumulative incidence curves were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods implemented in the survival package in R (v.3.8.6), with cumulative incidence calculated as 1 minus the survival probability. The AF-adjusted cumulative incidence of clinical obesity was estimated by multiplying the observed cumulative incidence of organ dysfunction by the corresponding AF estimates in each cohort.

For mortality risk analysis, participants were categorized into four groups: (1) no confirmed obesity and no organ dysfunction (reference group); (2) no confirmed obesity but with organ dysfunction; (3) confirmed obesity without organ dysfunction (preclinical obesity); or (4) confirmed obesity with organ dysfunction (clinical obesity). To evaluate whether the composite anthropometric criteria could detect high-risk individuals misclassified by BMI alone, we conducted the analysis of the association between obesity status and mortality in the following five groups: (1) no overweight or obesity (BMI < 24/25; reference group); (2) BMI-based overweight without CAD-obesity; (3) BMI-based overweight with CAD-obesity (that is, both elevated WC and elevated WHtR; this group can be viewed as the underdiagnosis of obesity by BMI alone); (4) BMI-based obesity without CAD-obesity (this group can be viewed as the overdiagnosis of obesity by BMI alone); and (5) BMI-based obesity with CAD-obesity. To further evaluate the effects of composite anthropometric criteria for excessive adiposity, participants were categorized into eight groups based on BMI-defined obesity status (yes, no), CAD-obesity status (yes, no) and presence of organ dysfunction (yes, no) at baseline.

Recent findings suggest that the association between obesity subtypes and mortality was estimated using the Cox proportional hazards models implemented in the survival package in R (v.3.8-6). Study-specific HRs and 95% CIs were pooled using fixed-effects meta-analysis implemented in the meta package in R (v.8.5.0). Time-at-risk extended from baseline to death or administrative censoring (31 December 2023 for the Kailuan Study, 19 December 2022 for the UKB and 31 December 2021 for the SIDIAP). Proportional hazards assumptions were verified using log–log survival plots. We performed several robustness checks, such as excluding deaths occurring within the first 2 or 5 years after baseline or including waist-to-hip ratio (≥0.90 for male and ≥0.85 for female individuals) as an additional criterion for central obesity. Stratified analyses by age groups (<60 and ≥60 years old), sex (male and female) and smoking status (never, former and current) were further performed to test the robustness of the results across subgroups of the participants.

In a recent development, all analyses were performed using SAS v.9.4 and R v.4.4.2. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05 (two-sided).

According to recent reports, results are shown as HRs and 95% CIs from the Cox proportional hazards model. The analyses included 137,792 participants with 17,642 deaths in the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants with 31,812 deaths in the UK Biobank and 51,269 participants with 2,338 deaths in the SIDIAP database. Points indicate HR point estimates and horizontal lines indicate 95% CIs. Models were adjusted for demographic factors (age and sex in all studies and, in addition, ethnicity in the UK Biobank), socio-economic status (marital status, educational level and household income in the Kailuan Study; employment, education and Townsend deprivation index in the UK Biobank; and MEDEA deprivation index in the SIDIAP) and lifestyle factors (smoking and alcohol consumption in all studies; physical activity in the Kailuan Study; and physical activity, diet quality and sleep duration in the UK Biobank). Interactions of obesity status with sex and age group were evaluated using joint Wald tests of the corresponding interaction terms; all Pinteraction values were <0.001. Pooled estimates were obtained using a fixed-effect meta-analysis model. All statistical tests were two-sided. In panel a, blue and orange represent men and female, respectively. In panel b, green and purple represent participants aged <60 years and ≥60 years, respectively. a, Sex-stratified analyses. b, Age-stratified analyses.

Scatter plots showing the association between BMI and WHtR among 137,795 participants in the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants in the UK Biobank, 218,841 participants in the All of Us Research Program and 51,269 participants in the SIDIAP database. Each point represents one participant. Points are coloured according to log-transformed point density. The solid line represents the fitted linear regression relationship between BMI and WHtR. Dashed vertical lines indicate BMI thresholds for overweight and obesity, defined as 24 and 28 kg/m² in the Kailuan Study and 25 and 30 kg/m² in the other cohorts. Dashed horizontal lines indicate the predicted WHtR values corresponding to these BMI thresholds based on the fitted linear regression models. Pearson correlation coefficients (r) between BMI and WHtR are shown within each panel. Pearson correlation tests were two-sided and statistically significant (P < 0.001). BMI was expressed as kg m−2, and WHtR was calculated as WC divided by height.

HRs and 95% CIs were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic factors, socio-economic status and lifestyle factors. The solid red lines indicate HRs, and the shaded areas indicate 95% CIs. The horizontal dashed line represents a HR of 1.0. Green dots indicate the reference values of WHtR in each cohort. Blue dashed curves indicate the density distribution of WHtR. Overall and nonlinear associations were assessed using two-sided Wald chi-square tests, with corresponding P values shown within each panel (Kailuan: Poverall = 5.99 × 10−29, Pnonlinear = 5.01 × 10−05; UK Biobank: Poverall = 4.75 × 10−253, Pnonlinear = 2.58 × 10−87; SIDIAP: Poverall = 9.47 × 10−20, Pnonlinear = 2.90 × 10−12).

  • The BBC article that I was reading, stated: “The blackout originated in the 1960s when Burnley chairman Bob Lord encouraged the EFL to oppose television coverage of 3pm Saturday matches.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The headline declared that Andy Burnham has urged caution on scrapping the 3pm Saturday TV blackout.

Ahead of this latest international break I was at the Fulham v Newcastle United game, the novelty of it being a rare 3pm kick-off for NUFC.

The BBC article that I was reading, stated: “The blackout originated in the 1960s when Burnley chairman Bob Lord encouraged the EFL to oppose television coverage of 3pm Saturday matches.”.

I understand the sentiments expressed by Andy Burnham, as he doesn’t want to be seen as upsetting the lower league clubs who are dependent on match day receipts and the peripheral spending.

However, when you look at the amount of games in the Premier League played outside the Saturday 3pm kick-off, you begin to wonder.

The working man’s game where you could rock up to St James’ Park with a belly full of ale for a 3pm kick-off and pay at the turnstiles are a thing of the past and long gone.

Take a look at the Newcastle United fixtures so far this season and you will see Fulham really was novelty.

In these first five months of the 2026-27 Premier League season only three 3pm Saturday kick-offs for Newcastle United, home to Hull and away to Fulham, plus Ipswich away next month.

All of these Premier League games played outside of the 3pm Saturday slot is a boon for lower league clubs. Due to technology, I can watch Newcastle play at 3pm on a Saturday even when I don’t get a ticket for the match.

But the 3pm Saturday kick-off is such a rarity it has become an irrelevance.

As the Newcastle United games are now shown at an increasingly ridiculous range of times, that frees up Saturday afternoon for me and my mates to go down to Dulwich Hamlet on a Saturday afternoon and have a pint of Peckham pale ale on the terracing while watching live football in the Isthmian Premier League.

So as me and my lad fail to get home tickets for Newcastle United on a regular basis now (no need for tiny violins), we are down the Hamlet on a Saturday afternoon with hundreds of other like minded Premier League team supporting people, who simply want to see live football kicking off at a proper time.

A shirt bearing Luke’s name will be placed on his seat in the stadium, providing a poignant symbol of the empty space left by his passing.

C&H encourage anyone attending the match, or anyone who sees Luke’s story online, to help spread the word and support the planned tribute.

On the 19th minute, every clap will be a reminder that Luke’s life touched many people and that his memory continues to live on through his family, friends, and fellow supporters.

Our thoughts are with everyone who knew and loved Luke.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newcastle United teenager Matheos Ferreira has made history in the colours of Brazil.
  • The exciting 18-year-old winger got his first ever call up for his country this month.
  • Matheos Ferreira named in the Brazil Under 20s squad for a double header with Peru.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newcastle United teenager Matheos Ferreira has made history in the colours of Brazil.

The exciting 18-year-old winger got his first ever call up for his country this month.

Matheos Ferreira named in the Brazil Under 20s squad for a double header with Peru.

He was an unused sub on Friday when the young Brazil stars won 2-0.

Then on Monday he made history, Matheos Ferreira becoming the first player developed at the Newcastle United Academy to go on to represent Brazil at international level.

The 18-year-old is from Berwick but is eligible to represent the country through his Brazilian father, Thiago.

Not only did Matheos Ferreira make his first ever start for the Brazil Under 20s on Monday, it only took him 14 minutes to score!

The United winger putting Brazil into the lead against Peru Under 20s in Belem.

— Bradley Robson (@bradrobson2605) November 17, 2026.

Matheos Ferreira seeing his dream international debut get even better when he also supplied an assist as the Brazil youngsters routed the opposition and won 9-0 against Peru.

Sources indicate that the Newcastle United Academy star talked to official NUFC club media from Brazil ahead of his debut: “I had to start training as soon as I got there but I think it’s shown how far I have come as a player because I wasn’t too nervous or anxious… I am doing the thing I love the most, playing football, and it was nice to get on the pitch and train with the squad. It’s been busy! The culture is completely different here but I really like it. We’re having to train in the evening as it is usually over 30 degrees during the day. Since the first training session, I’ve felt very welcome by the lads and the coaches as well.”.

Matheos Ferreira also qualifies to play potentially for England and Italy (his mam’s Italian).

The winger joined the Newcastle United Academy in 2020 after playing for Berwick Juniors and Cramlington Juniors and recalled the moment he found out he’d got his first Brazil call up: “My first reaction was just pure joy. I was so happy. My parents wanted to tell me first before I checked my phone but it was still a great moment to share with them, who were both very emotional. I think it’s a reward for how I’ve been playing but also how I’ve managed to conduct myself off the pitch with my recovery, willingness to learn and reflecting on how I can improve on the matches I’ve played in. It’s an amazing achievement but I don’t want this to be the last. I will keep pushing on and try to get that next call-up or progress into the first-team. Once I reach one level, it’s about getting to the next one. It doesn’t stop there. We’ve got the South American (Youth Football) Championship in January and the Under-20 World Cup is next year so I’m pushing really hard to try and get into both squads. I’m doing everything I can to try and make my international debut. It would mean a lot. I haven’t got this substantial pressure of needing to do well – I just want to get on that pitch, show what I can do and do what I love the most.”.

Matheos Ferreira remembering: “My first memory of Brazilian football would be my dad showing videos of Ronaldinho, R9 and Neymar,” he added. “The first game I watched live was at Wembley between England and Brazil and Neymar played. I think it finished goalless though! The interest they revealed me and the project they have was a substantial reason [to accept the call-up]. Brazil is a big country so to be recognised by them is amazing. It’s a big opportunity and an honour to represent them.”.

It has been revealed that the 18-year-old rising Newcastle United star is buzzing with how the 2026-27 season has kicked off, for club and country: “I’ve really enjoyed the start to this season. The coaches trust me as I’ve been playing in different positions for the Under-21s; wing-back, as a winger or a number ten. I think they know what I can provide for the team. I think its demonstrates the qualities I have. Playing as a right wing-back shows I can defend, put my body on the line and then it’s about showing my strengths going forward. I’ve embraced the challenges of switching positions, thinking about the tactical side of the game.”.

A brilliant moment on Monday for Matheos Ferreira and here’s to many more appearances (and goals!) in the colours of Brazil AND Newcastle United.

Industry observers note that how managers and fitness conditioning teams must dread these international breaks – a player coming back with a serious injury picked up on duty for the national side must be every coaches’ fear. it seems a case of ‘so far so good’ for West Ham’s “international brigade” with no reports filtering through to Hammers HQ of new issues.

Recent findings suggest that that does however leave the pre-existing condition: Manor Solomon’s frank admission to his national press will hardly reassure anyone at Rush Green. The winger has been struggling with a back injury and, according to sportwitness, this is neither a new concern nor one aggravated through too many games in the last window – which saw players asked to compete four times in twelve days for their nations:.

“My back is something I’ve been dealing with for many years, ever since I was a teenager. I felt it during Saturday’s game; when I joined the national team, I felt fine, but by Tuesday, it had got worse, and I couldn’t train,” he stated.

“Everyone knows how key the national team is to me and how hard it is for me to watch the team play while I’m not on the field. I hope I’ll be able to play on Tuesday.”.

Facing a late fitness test, it seems Solomon is putting caution to one side in his desperation to be part of the Israel national team to take on Austria tomorrow.

Sadly, there is nothing new here, the old ‘club v country‘ debate in which domestic football (paying the players’ massive wages) gets a lesser priority from a player who will stop at nothing and go through the pain to play for his country.

Solomon looked like the deal of the decade after his first couple of outings, having joined West Ham for a mere £5 million up front.

More disclosures about his back problems and many and varied other problems – which have led him to sit out an incredible 860 days since the start of his career in 2018 ( according to sportwitness) make the price look more understandable by the week.

It has been revealed that west Ham will have to cope with a player who has huge fitness complications but who doesn’t apparently, want to listen to his body, rather playing through the pain to represent his country. It’s not a combination that is likely preserve his longevity in the sport.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Mag Podcast Episode 17: Newcastle United’s 2015-16 relegation with lessons from the past.

Published: 16/11/2026 | Duration: 46 mins | Hosts: Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill & David Hutchinson.

In a recent development, in Episode 17 of The Mag Pod, we find Jamie, Simon, and Hutch discussing relegation, again! Special focus is on the 2015-16 season when the combined talents of Mike Ashley and Steve McClaren led to the club’s most recent drop to the Championship. So how does the current 2026-27 NUFC situation compare…?

You can play episode 17 on the audio player above or use your favourite podcast platforms including Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, YouTube, and Acast.

Industry observers note that listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! Join Jamie, Simon, and Hutch for unfiltered football debate.

Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill and David Hutchinson revisit Newcastle United’s 2015-16 relegation season under the ownership of Mike Ashley, examining the failures under Steve McClaren, the arrival of Rafa Benítez and whether there are lessons to be learned amid the concerns surrounding the current 2026-27 campaign.

The lads also discuss Newcastle United Women’s derby draw with Sunderland and the controversial travel restrictions for the upcoming Tyne-Wear derby.

In the second of three episodes this week, Hutch takes us through another particularly forgettable chapter in Newcastle United’s history. From a disappointing start to the season and a recruitment policy that prioritised potential over experience, to a divided dressing room and a lack of leadership on the pitch, there was no shortage of contributing factors to United’s downfall.

There’s a look back at the performances of Georginio Wijnaldum, Aleksandar Mitrović, Fabricio Coloccini and Moussa Sissoko, as well as some personal memories of the campaign, including a frustrating afternoon at Old Trafford and a particularly miserable pre-Christmas encounter with Aston Villa.

Could an earlier appointment of Rafa Benítez have saved Newcastle from relegation?

The lads discuss the importance of knowing when to make a managerial change, whilst considering the differences between the Newcastle United of a decade ago and the club today.

There’s also an assessment of the increasingly congested Premier League table, the importance of experienced players in a transitional squad and the heroes and villains of the 2015-16 season.

Naturally, a controversial Sergio Agüero goal brings about another argument between Jamie and Simon over the merits of VAR, with all the maturity listeners have come to expect.

Another nostalgic look at a period Newcastle United fans would rather forget, but one which offers plenty of talking points given the challenges facing United today.

Hamilton Academical 1 Ross County 2.

The depth of the descent of Hamilton Accies and Ross County would make it understandable if tickets for a fixture between the two carried warning about the bends when leaving Upcoming Douglas Park.

According to recent reports, the decompression sickness caused by emerging from a League One fixture for two sides who should be much higher must be severe. There may, however, be a positive prognosis.

Accies, despite their defeat, are whispering about stability, even though ‘legacy debt’ has to be faced, perhaps contested.

County, meanwhile, will not say it even in a whisper but Saturday’s victory takes them eight points clear at the top and heavily fancied for the title. The Staggies have one set of hooves in the Championship.

Sources indicate that scottish football, of course, does not restrict itself to the cliched fare of top of the table clashes so Newly introduced Douglas Park hosted a striker who is 39 later this month, a winger who was once a Scottish international, and a gentleman in the stands who once played against George Best. And a Ross County fan who regularly travels up from North Wales.

These exotic avenues demand to be explored but perennial questions about the financial health of the Accies had to be asked, too, after reports this week stating that hospitality packages at the club were being suspended.

An Accies fan feels the pain of defeat during Saturday's home loss to Ross County.

Allan Currie, chairman, answered them over a half-time pie.

‘We have come on in leaps and bounds but every week seems to throw up different challenges,’ he noted. ‘We have a level of debt that we have inherited and we are working with the creditors to try to navigate our way through that.’.

Matters on the field are positive, despite Saturday’s defeat.

It has been revealed that ‘The guys on the pitch, manager, and his staff have been unbelievable. Surviving in this league last season was phenomenal given what they were going through but it couldn’t be better now,’ he said. ‘Off the pitch, we are fighting with the different challenges we have. We are in a much better place even if we are not out the woods yet.’.

Asked what the level of pressure on him, he stated: ‘I am the guy on the ground but Rob Edwards is carrying out negotiations.’.

Edwards, through his Morley Group, took over the club earlier this year but has been sideswiped by a number of claims for payment. However, Currie has faith in the owner.

Industry observers note that ‘Without him, the club would not survive. Rob should take all the credit,’ he noted.

Asked what the short-term aims for the club were, Currie replied with a smile: ‘A goal in the second half would be good.’ A goal was scored but not for the Accies.

But the club remain in second place and the play-offs seem a more than reasonable prospect.

Ross County goalscorer Kieran Phillips battles with Hamilton's Kai Smutek.

Industry observers note that with 10 minutes to go, Hamilton brought on their latest signing. Barrie McKay, who has played for Scotland and scored for Rangers in a Scottish Cup semi-final against Celtic. His considerable achievements, though, paled in comparison to the subject of a casual conversation in the bar before the match.

‘I played against George Best,’ said Alan McDougall, with an air so off-hand one could have believed he was merely ordering another pint.

‘Yes, I played 200 games for the Accies. Davie McParland brought me here as a 21-year-old and I played for about six years. I went to Stranraer for a year and then went down south. I played against Best with the Accies.’.

In a recent development, the Northern Irish genius played for Hibernian in 1979-80. ‘He was well past his best and that was sad,’ noted McDougall. Best’s addiction to alcohol had taken a severe toll.

‘I came back to watch games five or six years ago,’ mentioned McDougall. ‘When the club went to Clyde, it destroyed me. What is fantastic is that the people that are now in control seem to be turning it around.’.

There was a mood of cautious optimism from other fans. ‘I have been a fan since forever, well the 1980s at least,’ said Gavin Fullarton. ‘I have seen this team in every division. I have seen them in the downs and downs. But I think we are going in the right direction. So far.’.

He added: ‘The new guys seem to know what they are doing. They are communicative.’.

There were 1,216 fans in the ground on Saturday with 300 stalwarts travelling down from the north. Colin Richardson, an Accies supporter, was asked why so many had stuck by the club.

‘It’s about loyalty,’ he noted. ‘You can’t pick and choose when you support your team. At the moment it is all about small steps. It has to be about stability.’.

According to recent reports, A Ross County fan had travelled up from North Wales. The journey to Scotland is a familiar one for Ian Ellson. ‘I have been all over Scotland to watch Ross County,’ he said. ‘Twenty years ago I visited Ross County and I was spoiled rotten. I decided to follow them.’.

According to recent reports, A social worker, he averages one visit a month. ‘I live and breathe Ross County,’ he stated. ‘This season we are going up.’.

Welsh Staggies fan Ian Elson and Englishman Ray Griffiths travelled far for Saturday's game.

Brian Graham would not be so bullish. He is 39 this month and has learned enough about football to know that predictions are made only to make the speaker seem foolish down the line.

Sources indicate that he was, though, expansive about what is happening at County. He joined the club for the second time in the summer after Stuart Kettlewell, the manager, convinced him of the ambitions in Dingwall.

‘This is a club where I have had success before so I know how good a club it can be,’ he noted. ‘It’s not been great for a couple of seasons but in the summer the manager set out his stall very early. It was about leaving egos at the door, building a togetherness and having a change of culture at the club. I think you are seeing that now.’.

The early signs were good for the striker who dropped down from Falkirk in the Premiership to play in Dingwall.

‘We had good pre-season performances against Aberdeen and Dundee and that was a solid building block,’ he said.

Brian Graham celebrates after scoring his 21st goal of the season for County.

Graham converted a first-half penalty to reach a tally of 21 goals this season and the Christmas trees are not up yet. ‘I get a lot of plaudits for scoring goals but others in the team are scoring a lot too,’ he remarked. ‘We are scoring team goals.’.

Has he set a target for the season? ‘When I came back I knew I had to score 13 to reach 50 goals for the club in two spells,’ he said. ‘I always set down targets in a wee black book but now I might need to readjust that.’.

Sources indicate that it was a night of adjustment for Darian MacKinnon. He had set a victory target but was condemned to accept defeat. He would not concede the league race was over. ‘We have to play them twice,’ he noted.

Industry observers note that he added ‘We are going in the right direction. The owners have put money in and they have backed us.’.

According to recent reports, asked to pinpoint a factor that has contributed to the team sitting second, he said: ‘The most positive thing for me this season is that this is now a good place to come into your work after the last three or four seasons. We are all actually enjoying coming to our work.’.

According to recent reports, there is work to be done on and off the pitch but the Accies are surviving. And that is the biggest result.

  • A total of 93 appearances – 42 as captain – and nineteen goals is a pretty stellar international career and for Soucek to have fought his way back from such a bad injury at the World Cup last summer highlights his fighting spirit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, time catches up with all of us, footballers just the same. Few are given much indication that the writing is on the wall, until suddenly that place which was automatically theirs is going to a younger, fitter, faster team mate – and then, suddenly, without a fanfare, almost always without even a ‘thank you’ –  it is over.

That, sadly, is likely to be the outcome for Czech stalwart and former captain Tomas Soucek who found himself an unused substitute last night after appearing for just five minutes in his countries’ previous game – during which Tornado Tom’s mistake in added time gifted Spain the injury time second goal in their 2 – 0 defeat of the Czechs.

A total of 93 appearances – 42 as captain – and nineteen goals is a pretty stellar international career and for Soucek to have fought his way back from such a bad injury at the World Cup last summer highlights his fighting spirit.

You’d think it unlikely that Soucek will make the squad in the March window, after being virtually discarded for the two Nations League games just gone – both of which his Czech Republic side lost.

Hopefully it’ll give the veteran a little more gusto to complete the job and see his West Ham side over the line and promoted back to the Premier League – which would be a fitting swan song for Soucek who’d be 32 next season and probably a bit-part player if the Hammers make it back to the top tier.

At least it’d mean domestically, he could go out at the top. Which he thoroughly deserves after more than 250 West Ham caps.
