Sources indicate that “Not good, because Q2 you know you are going to get through. You lose a set [of softs] in a qualifying that is so tight, where we are on the back foot. That is not good.”.

Sources indicate that lewis Hamilton claims this is the biggest crowd he has ever seen at Sepang, thanking the fans for making it here today. That is actually a bigger compliment than many watching at home may realise. The traffic this weekend has been horrendous. After 10 years without a race in Malaysia, during which time F1 has grown massively, I think they have forgotten how to do traffic management. Shuttles are inconsistent, taxis can’t get in/out, it’s taking forever just to reach the airport a few kilometres away - some fans have been braving the heat and walking. It took over two hours to get back into Kuala Lumpur last night (48km). My understanding is the Bahrainis are organising the race this year, while local forces are handling the traffic outside the circuit.

Sources indicate that “The car has been very good since last week. It is good to come back [from his wrist injury] at such a time and I am enjoying it, fighting for the top three. Even though it was not my finest qualifying session it is a good feeling.

“It is a bit unfortunate we take a penalty on a track where we are that fast but, from eighth, I am confident we can come through the field and come back for a good result.”.

Sources indicate that “I love this energy [from the crowd]. Big, big thank you to Malaysia for welcoming us. It is so hot here. I keep saying it, but that has made it a massive challenge for the tyres, the car, the mechanics in the garage. I am really, really thankful to my team. We made so many changes through all these practice sessions. Because the cars are sliding, the tyres are overheating, it was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot. To be able to close the gap to two or three tenths to Max [Verstappen], who has been so quick all weekend, is great, and I am so grateful.

“I am much happier with where the car is, but tomorrow is a completely different ballgame. Making these tyres last around this track, they are overheating from the get-go. Every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have makes a difference of how far you are going to go. I like to think we have got a good balance. Max was really quick on his long runs, so I will just try my best to hold onto him tomorrow.”.

It has been revealed that the screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he notes Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he mentioned. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external manufacturer who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”.

Ferrari this week have publicly backed their team principal Frederic Vasseur, amid speculation over the Frenchman’s position and comments made by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, who said the job at Ferrari would be a “dream job”. Ferrari, who sit second in the constructors’ standings, have not won the drivers’ championship since 2007 (Kimi Raikkonen) and the constructors’ since 2008. Here is a snippet from Tom Cary’s piece on the matter:.

In a hastily convened media call on Tuesday morning, Maria Conti, Ferrari’s chief communication officer, remarked the Scuderia had decided to concern a vote of confidence in Vasseur in response “not just to the story of Mr Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred”.

“Ferrari has made its choices,” Conti stated. “We have confidence – full confidence – in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

“At this time, it’s really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.”.

In a recent development, “It is great to be back [in Malaysia]. I am really enjoying the track. We have had some wonderful races here over time. It is actually the 20th time we have been here, it started in 1999, and it is really exciting to be back. I really enjoyed getting out on the track and watching the cars closely.

“The drivers are super fit and they have some cooling but it is not easy. But you almost cannot get enough fluid through your body before your stomach gives up. Having this race and Singapore back-to-back increases that challenge.”.

Especially with the big upgrade they have brought this weekend, Mercedes’ lead at the summit is looking unassailable right now.

In a recent development, almost nine years ago to the day, Max Verstappen took just his second race victory in Formula 1. Lewis Hamilton, who took pole position, and Daniel Ricciardo joined Verstappen on the podium. Despite being nine years ago, plenty of drivers still on the grid were racing that weekend. In a recent development, with Russell winning in Baku and Antonelli finishing fifth, the latter’s championship lead was cut to 66 points. If Russell is going to usurp his teammate, he is going to need a few more similar results to last weekend due to the size of Antonelli’s lead. If Antonelli were to suffer a retirement, then that completely changes the outlook.

Formula One returns to Malaysia for round 16 of the season for the Bahrain Grand Prix. That probably sounds strange but after the Bahrain Grand Prix was originally postponed in March, F1 reinstated it to the calendar with Malaysia hosting it because of the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite being held in Malaysia, Bahrain have retained the naming rights for the event, which is officially known as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The last time Formula One was in Malaysia was nine years ago back in 2017, when a young whippersnapper named Max Verstappen, still four years away from winning his first world championship, claimed just his second victory.

Last time out around the streets of Baku, Mercedes’ George Russell claimed victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Verstappen by just a tenth of a second. That was Russell’s first grand prix win since June and cuts his team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ standings to 66 points. Antonelli had a challenging weekend in Baku, starting 16th after a crash in qualifying and coming home in fifth to see his championship lead to Russell cut by 15 points.

Recent findings suggest that verstappen was quickest in first practice yesterday, with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fastest in second practice. Earlier today, championship leader Antonelli was nearly three tenths clear of the field in third practice. Mercedes, 160 points clear at the top of the constructors’ standings, have brought significant upgrades this weekend, which includes a new floor, rear suspension and rear corner. It is the team’s first significant car upgrade since the Canadian Grand at the end of May.

In a recent development, this race in Malaysia represents the second leg of the season’s first flyaway triple header, with the Singapore Grand Prix to come next weekend, so the demands on the teams and the drivers are incredibly high. Qualifying from Sepang gets under way at 9am (GMT).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this, the second week of the second international break of the season, there’s an understandable eagerness amongst fans to get back to the serious business of league football again this coming weekend.

However there is still a crucial fixture tonight, before the autumn internationals are concluded, in which West Ham supporters should take an interest.

Greece against Serbia in the UEFA Nations League Group A hardly sets the pulse racing as a neutral: It’s normally a game I could happily ignore but it takes on a special meaning after West Ham’s Dinos Mavropanos performed so poorly in the crushing 7 – 0 defeat by the Netherlands last time out.

Consequently I will be taking a bit of an interest in this somewhat obscure game to see how West Ham’s number 15 is looking after such a demoralising result three days ago,.

West Ham need Mavropanos to return having put the 7 – 0 thrashing firmly behind him.

West Ham’s main man took a bit of a pasting in the Greek media after the game, in what was described as the ‘blackest night‘ for Greek football.

West Ham, already without Maximilian Kilman, remember, banned for the upcoming Saturday tie against Preston North End, will be keeping everything crossed that their one remaining senior centre-back has a solid evening facing up to the likes of Mitrovic, Jovic and co.

Scott Parker already has a selection dilemma over bringing in teenager Airidas Golambeckis or loanee Morato to replace Kilman.

The last thing he or West Ham need is another shaky Mavropanos performance tonight and a return to the ‘Mavropanic’ days of the past – which another heavy defeat could usher back in.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have been reading lately, with interest, the conversations surrounding the return of Bruno Guimaraes to St James’ Park this coming weekend (Saturday 21st November).

Opinion seems to be split as to what kind of reception our former captain should receive if he is selected to face us on Saturday evening.

Since leaving Newcastle United, Bruno Guimaraes hasn’t been an automatic starter, so we may not have the chance to show him our collective feelings either way.

From what I am reading the camp seems to be split directly down the middle between “Bruno Guimaraes is a hero who led us to our first silverware in decades”, to “Bruno Guimaraes is a traitor who went all out to manufacture a move away from the club.”.

Looking back now at the summer dealings it’s easier to reflect on what happened and why the players who left, did.

In my opinion , it was only a matter of time before Sandro left us, his heart never seemed in the Northeast, neither does it in North London to be honest, the only time I think we will see him truly happy is when he is plying his trade back in Italy, unfortunately for him it doesn’t look as if Italian football could subsidise that kind of financial arrangement.

Again, in my opinion the same can be stated about Anthony Gordon, I liked the lad but also got the impression he thought he was destined for a bigger club, something which was proven to be true.

In a recent development, I just got the impression he thought he was too big a name for the club and it was a matter of time before he left. The fact he went abroad seemed to make the move slightly more palatable as a Newcastle fan.

And on to Bruno, I love(d) the bloke, I was stood in the away section of the Stadium of light, with 7,000 others, 3-0 up and watched him slide tackle on our own goal line and celebrate as if he had scored.

Recent findings suggest that I loved his passion and enthusiasm for the game and the Toon. He could drive and win a game single handedly by grabbing the team by the scruff of the neck and pushing the team forward.

I loved his speech at the presentation in Leases Park and the way he appreciated the character of the Northeast.

Industry observers note that will I boo him if he plays on Saturday? 100%. This is not out of spite; I take this decision more so on a few factors.

Bruno Guimaraes is a confidence player; we have seen this ourselves over the years. We know he feels bad about leaving, he has made a few statements leading up to the game about the toughest decision he has had to make-blah blah blah etc.

It has been revealed that but, he went out of his way to hire a super-agent in Kia Joorabchian to help get a move away. Not the actions of a player in love with the glorious Northeast.

He had opportunities to soften the blow leaving, many times over the course of the 2026 World Cup, but chose the cowards way out with total silence, despite the obvious affect it would have on the fans.

Let’s get at him, rattle him, affect his confidence, and take the roof off every time Dan Burn cuts him in half, maybe that will be enough to unsettle him and his teammates.

Newcastle United are in a transitional period as a team, but I still feel on a Saturday evening kick off, with a crowd fuelled with day drinking we can beat anyone..

Maybe spare applause for Bruno Guimaraes at the end for his service to the club, I will.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the international break, Saturday’s clash with Preston North End feels like a pivotal moment in West Ham’s season. The Hammers desperately need to start climbing the table, and while promotion remains within reach, time is quickly becoming a factor.

Sources indicate that promotion from the Championship is not won on reputation alone. West Ham began the season as the bookmakers’ favourites for automatic promotion, but that tag has quietly disappeared.

Recent findings suggest that the dismissal of Nuno and the appointment of Scott Parker signalled a fresh start, although our new manager has had limited time with the squad before the break. What already seems evident, however, is that West Ham’s struggles stem from structural concerns rather than shortcomings of individual players.

Kretinsky was not prepared to back Espirito Santo any longer -his tactics and playing style were not working.

It has been revealed that parker will be fully aware of the challenges facing his side. The Championship is a division where possession statistics mean very little unless they are backed up by purpose, intensity and results.

In a recent development, goals have not been the problem. Defensive frailties have been the far greater concern. Playing  Morato at left back never looked convincing, and Saturday’s team selection will be fascinating. With Kilman unavailable due to suspension, Parker must decide whether to pair Mavropanos with Golambekis or Morato.

In a recent development, the absence of a prolific, out-and-out goalscorer has also raised questions. Joel Piroe was recruited to fill that role and, on paper, the logic was sound. He is a proven Championship striker. Four goals and two assists in 14 appearances suggest he is moving in the right direction, but when compared to the division’s leading scorer, Will Lankshear, who has 13 goals, the gap is impossible to ignore.

Ironically, West Ham are the Championship’s leading scorers with 37 goals. Encouragingly, those goals are coming from all areas of the pitch rather than relying on a single player. Yet, there is one player, Jarrod Bowen who has been central to that success, contributing seven goals and leading the league’s assist charts with seven in fifteen matches.

He will go if the club don’t secure promotion, an inevitable outcome should the club not succeed this season.

Perhaps the biggest challenge for West Ham, is psychological.

West Ham arrived in the Championship expecting results to come naturally. As fans we expected an automatic promotion place.

At times this season, West Ham have looked weighed down by expectation. Instead of playing with the confidence of promotion contenders, the team have often appeared nervous and overly cautious, afraid of making costly mistakes.

Scott Parker’s biggest task may not be tactical at all. He must build a mentality centred on resilience and belief rather than entitlement.

If he can transform West Ham into a side that is more aggressive, more robust and better suited to the harsh realities of Championship football, promotion is still very much achievable.

According to recent reports, if he cannot, the club’s stay in the second tier could last far longer than anyone at the London Stadium ever imagined. Saturday could be the first real indication of which path they are heading down.

Long-serving goalkeeper Alisson Becker is into the final year of his contract at Anfield, but he recently expressed his desire to extend his stay at the club, and his agent has reportedly entered ‘preliminary talks’ with LFC chiefs over a prospective new deal.

With the Brazilian’s status as number 1 firmly intact, it leaves Giorgi Mamardashvili playing a backup role and having to be patient for opportunities, a situation that he might feel a compulsion to change in the foreseeable future.

In a video on his eponymous YouTube channel, Romano outlined that the Georgian mightn’t be prepared to wait for his chance for much longer if Alisson were to extend his contract.

Recent findings suggest that the transfer reporter said: “Liverpool are no longer masters of Alisson’s destiny, let’s put it that way. Last summer they were able to say, ‘Stay with us, we’ll extend for another year, we’ll activate the option.’ Now that option has expired, so Alisson can decide his future.

Sources indicate that “There is certainly a possibility that Alisson will remain at Liverpool. However, the situation involving him and Giorgi Mamardashvili is becoming increasingly complicated.

Industry observers note that “This is because Mamardashvili is not a player who wants to remain a backup goalkeeper indefinitely. He is playing second fiddle while waiting for the door to open for a starting spot at Liverpool and at some point, a decision will have to be made.”.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Romano’s information echoes that of James Pearce a few weeks ago when the latter indicated that, if Alisson were to stay put, his understudy wouldn’t accept a third season of playing backup to the Brazil veteran.

The role of a second-choice goalkeeper is a peculiar one. They’re only one twist of fate away from getting what could be their big break, but they could be left waiting months (if not years) for that sliding doors moment.

Mamardashvili hasn’t yet managed to seriously challenge our number 1 for a place in the starting XI, but the Georgian has produced some strong performances in the Carabao Cup this season, including one world-class save against Tottenham in the third round in September.

Even his status as Alisson’s immediate deputy could come under threat from next year once Lucca Brughmans arrives from Genk, although that chain of command would be contingent on the Brazilian’s future at Liverpool.

We can see it from Mamardashvili’s perspective – he’s 26 now and won’t want to fritter away too much of his career warming the bench – but it’s essential for the Reds to have a solid succession strategy in place for life after their long-serving number 1, whose world-class presence will be extremely difficult to replace.

In a recent development, west Ham United’s window of opportunity to acquire their rented home for next to nothing appears to be fading. With £20 million of losses each year, the ground is a massive white elephant with the main tenant paying next to nothing for it’s bullet proof lease.

Industry observers note that former vice Chair Karren Brady, say what you like about her,  did at least negotiate the deal of the century giving West Ham a rock solid indestructible tenancy for generations to come. As the club were relegated, so the rent diminished leaving the owners to pick up the tab for West Ham’s failure on the pitch: An estimated £2.5 million each year is added to the tax payer burden thanks to the clause existing to reduce costs when West Ham dropped out of the Premier League.

Opportunities existed this summer, so we were told,  for the club to negotiate to buy the stadium, with suggestions that it would take £50 million for the deal to be done.

In the apparent lack of any take up by West Ham’s shareholders, the stadium owners have sought to bump up the former Olympic venue’s value in the meantime, by seeking to increase revenues through obtaining permission from Newham Council for a wider array of entertainment. According to London.stadium.com that effort has paid dividends:.

Sources indicate that meaning the revenue which can be generated from the Stadium will be significantly higher, theoretically at least increasing its value and likely heading off West Ham’s options of acquiring it for next to nothing. Possibly.

It has been revealed that west Ham’s London Stadium at night: There’ll be more events, louder music and bigger attendances – still won’t make a profit though. Just saying.

However the huge maintenance costs and temporary nature of the upper part of the structure means that even with consent for more events, bigger attendances and louder music, London Stadium is never going to become a lucrative, marketable venue in it’s current configuration.

Someone is going to have to spend hundreds of millions of pounds on fixing it: Like a giant pass-the-parcel game with a huge ticking time bomb of debt at the core of the fancy wrapping, neither West Ham nor the owners want to be left holding the bill when the music stops.

The difference is, the status quo favours the club, not the Greater London Authority who, as it stands, will find it pretty near impossible to turn a profit even with fresh approvals granted and new events lined up. And as every year passes, the need to spend substantial, big money on maintenance grows greater. In this instance, West Ham’s board biding their time and kicking it into the long grass for a few years yet is probably the shrewdest course of action. From the football club’s perspective.

Liverpool are reportedly keen for Ifeanyi Ndukwe to continue his development on loan with Levante in Spain, despite the player now being eligible for a UK work permit.

The 18-year-old was a revelation for the Reds in pre-season but, at the time, he didn’t meet the criteria to play competitively in England and was subsequently dispatched to the LaLiga outfit for this season.

He’s continued to perform impressively for Los Azulgranas, and there were reports last month of his agents arranging to discuss the possibility of a January recall to Anfield.

According to Graeme Bailey for TEAMtalk, Liverpool are convinced that Ndukwe could break into their first-team setup next year and view him as ‘hugely important’ for their long-term aims.

Although he could theoretically be recalled in January, the Reds’ preference is for him to remain with Levante for the rest of his season and proceed with his development there.

That hasn’t stopped some Premier League clubs from enquiring about his availability for a loan move for the second half of the campaign to give him a first taste of English top-flight football.

It has been revealed that want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Having had to wait until October for his first start for Levante, Ndukwe was then included from the first whistle in all six of their LaLiga games since the extended international break earlier in the autumn (Transfermarkt).

Luis Castro demonstrably has faith in the Austrian teenager, whose performances on loan have earned praise from the Spanish media, although the occasional error has served as a reminder that he’s still developing and will have off-days as part of that.

While Premier League exposure would be a quite informative barometer of the youngster’s readiness for the Liverpool first team, we’d be in favour of him continuing with Levante if he’s enjoying regular game-time there.

At the moment Ndukwe is featuring regularly in one of Europe’s foremost domestic leagues, and doing so with a club where media attention and scrutiny is comparatively sparse, thus keeping him away from the harshest of exposure.

He must be doing plenty right to have English top-flight clubs asking about taking him on loan in the winter. If that’s the case, then the current initiative seems to be working, and we see no reason to deviate from that any time soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, former West Ham United vice-chair Karren Brady has debuted a new commercial agency alongside fellow former Hammers director Nathan Thompson, specialising in sponsorship, hospitality and commercial strategy. The business, craetively called Brady Thompson, aims to help organisations unlock what its founders describe as hundreds of millions of pounds in untapped commercial value.

According to City AM, the pair have reunited just seven months after departing West Ham, with Brady talking enthusiastically about the enormous commercial opportunities available in sport and entertainment.

It has been revealed that I have to say, I find it absolutely incredible that Brady has any sort of influence or clout in a business focusing on sponsorship, hospitality and commercial strategy, considering the Baroness was vice-chair when West Ham recorded losses of £104.2m in their last published accounting period. And that’s before we get onto the rather awkward subject of the London Stadium.

West Ham’s accounts for the financial year ending May 2025 revealed a pre-tax loss of £104.2m, a remarkable turnaround from the previous year’s £57.2m profit.

In a recent development, now, clearly, not every penny of that loss can be attributed to Karren Brady. Football finances are complicated, and player recruitment, wages, transfer dealings and league performance all have a significant impact.

But she was one of the most senior executives at the football club, and surely the financial performance of the business has to form part of any assessment of her commercial legacy.

Indeed, Claret & Hugh previously reported that Brady had even become directly involved in negotiating transfers during the January 2026 window.

I’ve questioned the timing of her departure before, particularly given the financial difficulties and footballing problems that were developing towards the end of her time at the club.

So forgive me if I’m not immediately convinced by the idea that the same leadership can now teach other organisations how to maximise their commercial potential.

But perhaps the biggest irony of all is the decision to launch an agency specialising in sponsorship when, after ten years at the London Stadium, West Ham and the stadium authorities collectively failed to secure a naming-rights partner for the former Olympic venue.

A Premier League football club, based in London, playing in a stadium with a capacity of more than 60,000, and after a decade nobody managed to get a naming-rights deal over the line.

Recent findings suggest that that wasn’t solely Brady’s responsibility, of course. The London Legacy Development Corporation controlled the stadium’s commercial arrangements, and there were disagreements about the value of any potential deal.

In fact, Brady herself pressed the stadium authorities to pursue naming rights, and the London Assembly has documented correspondence in which she expressed West Ham’s willingness to help secure an agreement.

Nevertheless, the outcome remains the same.

As Claret & Hugh reported last year, the stadium operators were warning that a naming-rights agreement might not materialise until 2028 or beyond.

And in my previous article about the missing £4m sponsorship opportunity, I argued that the failure to secure a partner when the stadium first opened had allowed the London Stadium name to become so established that selling it now would be considerably more difficult.

That is hardly a ringing endorsement of the commercial arrangements surrounding West Ham’s move from Upton Park.

Brady told City AM that unlocking commercial opportunities required imagination, experience, relationships and the willingness to challenge convention.

Nathan Thompson, meanwhile, pointed to his experience negotiating commercial deals from different sides of the boardroom.

I’m sure both have considerable contacts within the business world, and there’s no doubt Brady has spent decades operating at decent levels of football administration.

According to recent reports, but contacts and experience are one thing. Results are another.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps the venture will prove enormously successful. Perhaps they’ll secure the sort of sponsorship agreements that other sporting organisations have struggled to attract.

However, from a West Ham supporter’s perspective, it is difficult to look beyond the £104m loss, the club’s subsequent relegation and the decade-long failure to find a stadium naming-rights sponsor.

When somebody starts offering advice about how to unlock hundreds of millions of pounds in commercial value, I don’t think it’s unreasonable to ask why so much potential remained untapped at the football club they helped run for 16 years.

But hey, if all else fails the latest firm name of Brady Thompson does sound like excellent branding for a luxury soap should they wish to diversify.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rafael Benitez has opened up about the ‘difficult’ time that he had at Liverpool during the damaging ownership era of Tom Hicks and George Gillett.

The American businessmen bought the Merseyside club in 2007 amid grandiose promises about a fresh stadium in Stanley Park (‘a spade in the ground within 60 days’, and all that), but they promptly became hugely unpopular figures among the fan base.

As the duo ultimately fell out with one another amid a period of civil war at the club, debts mounted to the extent that LFC was on the brink of administration in 2010 before they were ousted by a takeover from Fresh England Sports Ventures (now Fenway Sports Group).

In an interview with The Athletic, Benitez was asked if he ever thought back to what could’ve been for Liverpool had it not been for the damaging ownership of Hicks and Gillett, throughout which time the Spaniard kept the club challenging for major silverware.

The former Reds boss reflected: “Yes, 100%. When Hicks and Gillett came, they changed the approach. All the things you did for the benefit of the club, they had different ideas. I realised, and the fans realised later, that something was wrong. They didn’t have experience of football.

It has been revealed that “I remember speaking to Gillett once in London after we played Tottenham. He said: ‘We will give you money and then next season you’ll get us into the play-offs.’ I had to tell him there were no play-offs.

“They thought maybe: ‘Rafa is a threat.’ That period was difficult, but all I ever wanted was the best for the club.”.

(Photo by Oli Scarff/Getty Images).

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Benitez’s final season at Liverpool in 2009/10 was a major disappointment, with the Reds expected to challenge for the title but slumping to a seventh-place finish, and there was a prevailing sentiment that the time was right for a change in the dugout.

However, as the extent of the damage done by Hicks and Gillett became clear in subsequent months and years, the latter part of the Spaniard’s managerial reign has come to be viewed in a much kinder light.

He was left with an impossible job of trying to achieve success on the pitch while all sorts of strife was going on in the background, slowly eating away at the club until John Henry rode to the rescue in October 2010.

Benitez’s time at Liverpool may have ended on a low ebb, but he remains a greatly appreciated figure among the fans for delivering Champions League glory in Istanbul and getting the Reds back to being a competitive force domestically and on the continent, even if the Premier League eluded him.

Had it not been for the incompetence of those at ownership level, who knows just how much more the Spaniard could’ve achieved at Anfield in the late 2000s and possibly into the 2010s?

#14593. Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart

Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 52 min read (10366 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~52 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase1,2.
  • It has been revealed that DNA lesion bypass by leading-strand repriming was demonstrated for the core Escherichia coli replisome, in which primer synthesis is performed by the primase also responsible for lagging-strand replication12,13.
  • cerevisiae, humans have an additional primase called PRIMPOL7,8,9.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase1,2. Failure to efficiently restart and/or protect stalled replication forks is a major source of genomic instability3,4,5,6. Stalled forks can be restarted by a variety of mechanisms, including repriming downstream of the impediment4. In human cells, the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL promotes fork progression during replication stress7,8,9,10, but how its activity is coordinated by the replisome is unresolved. Here, by reconstituting replication fork stalling and restart with purified human proteins, we show that the CMG helicase directs PRIMPOL for efficient replication fork restart. Unexpectedly, the interaction between PRIMPOL and replication protein A9,11 is not critical for fork restart in this system. We show that PRIMPOL binds directly to CMG, and a cryo-electron microscopy structure illustrates how this targets PRIMPOL specifically for leading-strand priming to minimize the size of post-replicative gaps. Ablating the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction abolishes fork restart in vitro and PRIMPOL-dependent DNA damage tolerance in human cells. Our work establishes PRIMPOL as an integrated component of the human replisome dedicated to leading-strand priming.

It has been revealed that DNA lesion bypass by leading-strand repriming was demonstrated for the core Escherichia coli replisome, in which primer synthesis is performed by the primase also responsible for lagging-strand replication12,13. By contrast, eukaryotic replisomes reconstituted from purified Saccharomyces cerevisiae proteins cannot efficiently resume synthesis downstream of leading-strand lesions1 because the Pol α–primase complex that is responsible for priming each Okazaki fragment is targeted to the lagging-strand template14. This targeting mechanism is conserved in the human replisome14, indicating that inefficient priming on the leading strand by Pol α–primase is a universal feature of eukaryotic replisomes.

Unlike S. cerevisiae, humans have an additional primase called PRIMPOL7,8,9. PRIMPOL is a 560-amino-acid (aa) monomeric enzyme comprising a 21-aa amino-terminal helix of unknown function, an archaeo-eukaryotic primase (AEP) domain, a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding zinc-finger (ZnF) and two C-terminal replication protein A (RPA) binding motifs (RBMs)6,15. Extensive evidence from human, mouse and chicken cell lines highlights that PRIMPOL promotes replication fork progression under conditions that stall replicative DNA polymerases8,9,10 and that this requires PRIMPOL primase activity10,16,17,18, leading to the formation of daughter-strand gaps5,19. Current models indicate that PRIMPOL is recruited to replication forks through a direct interaction with RPA9,11,16. However, because RPA is constitutively associated with the lagging-strand template, it is unclear whether this mode of recruitment is sufficient for efficient PRIMPOL priming on the leading strand, or whether an additional mechanism directs PRIMPOL specifically to the leading-strand template to rescue stalled replication forks.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate leading-strand repriming by PRIMPOL in the context of the replisome, we leveraged a system that we recently developed to assemble fast and efficient human replisomes from purified proteins20. In this approach, CMG is first loaded onto the forked end of a 9.7-kb DNA template before additional proteins are added to assemble replisomes that perform robust leading- and lagging-strand DNA replication (Fig. 1a). Pol ε performs the bulk of leading-strand synthesis, whereas Pol α–primase and Pol δ replicate the lagging strand. RFC and CTF18-RFC load the polymerase processivity factor PCNA onto the lagging and leading strands, respectively, and TIMELESS (TIM)–TIPIN, CLASPIN and AND1 associate with CMG to promote rapid replisome progression20. To monitor fork stalling and restart, a single cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer (CPD)—an key ultraviolet (UV)-induced DNA lesion and a potent block to replicative polymerases—was introduced to the leading-strand template 3.5 kb from the forked end1,20.

a, Schematic of the forked-DNA replication assay with a template containing a leading-strand CPD lesion. b, Time course of a replication assay on the leading-strand CPD template in the absence or presence of PRIMPOL. c, Two-dimensional gel analysis of a 30-min replication reaction in the presence of PRIMPOL.

Figure 1b shows that the CPD is a potent block to leading-strand DNA synthesis (3.5-kb stall lead product in denaturing gel), which causes replication forks to stall, as visualized by the slowly migrating species in the native gel (stalled fork). Similar replisome behaviour was observed when the CPD was substituted for a tetrahydrofuran abasic site (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Addition of PRIMPOL caused a reduction in the stalled fork population and the accumulation of full-length products in the native gel, concomitant with the appearance of an approximately 6.2-kb product in the denaturing gel (Fig. 1b, lanes 5–8, restart lead product). This result strongly indicated that PRIMPOL was promoting fork restart by leading-strand repriming. To confirm that the 6.2-kb products resulted from leading-strand repriming, products were analysed by two-dimensional gel electrophoresis (Fig. 1c). This demonstrated that the 6.2-kb products were exclusively associated with the full-length product in the native gel and were roughly twice as intense as the 3.5-kb stall leading-strand product, as expected for bona fide restart products. Moreover, replication of the CPD template in the presence of a primase-defective PRIMPOL mutant (ZnFD2A)10 generated only stalled leading strands and Okazaki fragments (Extended Data Fig. 1b). These data illustrate the successful reconstitution of replication fork restart by leading-strand repriming using purified human proteins.

Industry observers note that replication fork restart also occurred efficiently after polymerase stalling at an abasic site (Extended Data Fig. 1c), suggesting that the mechanism of repriming is agnostic to the chemical nature of the initial blocking lesion. Restart also occurred independently of Pol δ (Extended Data Fig. 1d) and Pol α–primase (Extended Data Fig. 1c), illustrating that only Pol ε is required to extend the primer made by PRIMPOL in this system. Therefore, unless stated, Pol δ is omitted from subsequent experiments to avoid complications from strand-displacement synthesis.

According to recent reports, unlike Pol α–primase, which has a strong preference for rNTPs for primer synthesis21, following the 5′ rNTP, PRIMPOL incorporates dNTPs with a much higher efficiency than rNTPs owing to a sugar discrimination mechanism7,8,22. Consistent with these properties, omitting GTP, CTP and UTP did not compromise leading-strand restart (Extended Data Fig. 1e, compare lanes 7 and 8), indicating that ATP is sufficient for primer initiation in these assays. However, despite previous reports that manganese stimulates PRIMPOL priming activity in vitro8, its addition did not enhance the efficiency of restart (Extended Data Fig. 1f).

In a recent development, the observation that restart products were close to their maximum possible length (6.2 kb) indicated that they were initiated a very short distance from the lesion. To obtain a high-resolution view of leading-strand restart, we devised a strategy to map priming sites at near single-nucleotide resolution (Fig. 2a). To do so, products were post-replicatively digested with restriction enzymes that cut upstream and downstream of the lesion to liberate fragments that could be resolved in polyacrylamide sequencing gels. Figure 2b shows that, apart from the stalled leading strand and a minor population of read-through products, a ladder of products was generated upon digestion of the PRIMPOL-containing reaction (lane 4). We conclude that each band in the ladder corresponds to a unique leading-strand repriming site. Notably, most of the PRIMPOL-dependent primers used to restart replication were synthesized within 50 nucleotides of the CPD, even when the PRIMPOL concentration was reduced to 5 nM (Extended Data Fig. 2a). An indistinguishable ladder pattern was observed following replication of the abasic site template (Extended Data Fig. 2b), showing that the chemical nature of the DNA lesion plays no part in priming site specification. Because CMG is likely to continue slowly unwinding DNA after polymerase stalling1,2, these data indicate that PRIMPOL activity is targeted to the leading-strand template immediately after polymerase stalling, which limits the size of the daughter-strand gap to generally <50 nucleotides on this template.

a, Schematic of the predicted products generated from digestion of replication products with SalI and NruI. b, Urea polyacrylamide gel of a 40-min replication reaction processed as in a. c, Schematic of the DNA template in which a 162-nt sequence after the CPD was replaced with an alternative sequence. d, Urea polyacrylamide gel of a 40-min replication reaction containing PRIMPOL, processed as in a. Pol δ was omitted from the experiments in b and d. Und, undamaged.

Previous work established that PRIMPOL exhibits sequence preferences for the initiation of primer synthesis23,24,25. We therefore reasoned that the distinct pattern of restart products in our experiments was a consequence of the DNA sequence downstream of the CPD. To test this, we modified a 162-nt region downstream of the CPD (Fig. 2c). Replication of this modified template in the presence of PRIMPOL generated a distinct pattern of restart products to those from the original CPD template (Fig. 2d, compare lanes 3 and 4). This shows that leading-strand repriming by PRIMPOL in the context of the human replisome is modulated by DNA sequence. Importantly, despite the altered sequence, most restart products were again initiated within <50 nucleotides of the CPD, with one prominent product initiated about 100 nt from the CPD (Fig. 2d, lane 4). This is consistent with both templates containing multiple close matches to the preferred tri-nucleotide primer initiation sequence for PRIMPOL25.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery that PRIMPOL-mediated repriming occurred a short distance from the CPD on two distinct templates suggested that an efficient mechanism directs PRIMPOL to the exposed leading-strand template. We hypothesized that this was mediated by the RBMs in the PRIMPOL C terminus11, recruiting PRIMPOL to RPA bound to the leading-strand template following polymerase stalling at the CPD and continued template unwinding by CMG. To examine this, we generated two PRIMPOL mutants defective in RPA binding: one lacking both RBMs and the other carrying a mutant in RBM-A (RBM-ARA) that abolished PRIMPOL localization to chromatin in human cells11 (Fig. 3a). Figure 3b shows that both PRIMPOL mutants promoted leading-strand restart with comparable efficiency to wild-type PRIMPOL. Moreover, analysis of restart products demonstrated that both mutants exhibited the same repriming site pattern as wild-type PRIMPOL (Fig. 3c). We conclude that RBM-mediated interactions between PRIMPOL and RPA are non-essential for replication fork restart with reconstituted human replisomes.

Products were digested post-replicatively with SalI and NruI. d, Denaturing agarose gel analysis of a 40-min replication reaction with dropouts of non-essential replisome components on undamaged and CPD templates in the presence of PRIMPOL. e, Silver-stained SDS–PAGE analysis of a pull-down experiment with the indicated proteins. WT, wild type.

The non-essentiality of the PRIMPOL RBMs for fork restart, together with the very close proximity of repriming to the lesion, prompted us to explore the idea that PRIMPOL might be directed to stalled forks through an interaction with the core replisome. Omission of all non-essential core replisome components individually did not abolish leading-strand restart (Fig. 3d). We therefore hypothesized that PRIMPOL might be recruited directly by the CMG helicase. Consistent with this idea, the pull-down experiment in Fig. 3e shows that PRIMPOL interacts specifically with CMG.

Sources indicate that to investigate how PRIMPOL is recruited to CMG, and how this might facilitate efficient leading-strand repriming, we determined a structure of PRIMPOL bound to CMG by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) (Extended Data Fig. 3a–d and Extended Data Table 1). Well-resolved cryo-EM density was recovered for the PRIMPOL AEP domain alongside the ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7 that form part of the C-terminal tier (C-tier) of the two-tiered hexameric MCM ring (Fig. 4a,b). This arrangement is mediated by a conserved 21-aa α-helix at the N terminus of PRIMPOL binding to MCM7 and an approximately 20-aa loop immediately downstream of the helix that is sandwiched between a shallow groove on MCM4 and the PRIMPOL AEP domain (Fig. 4b,c and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). The PRIMPOL AEP domain is positioned laterally adjacent to the exit of the MCM central pore, through which the unwound leading-strand template emerges. Moreover, superimposing the crystal structure of PRIMPOL bound to primer-template DNA26 onto the AEP domain in our structure demonstrates that its catalytic core is oriented to support primer synthesis directly as template DNA is fed from CMG (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 4c).

The protein structure shown is the CMG–PRIMPOL structure from this study. The DNA in the model was generated by superpositioning the PRIMPOL–DNA structure (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 5L2X) and CMG-forked DNA structure (PDB: 7PFO) onto the PRIMPOL–CMG structure in this study.

It has been revealed that guided by our cryo-EM structure, to evaluate the role of the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction in replication fork restart, we removed the first 39 aa of PRIMPOL (PRIMPOL∆1–39) (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 5a). Figure 5b shows that wild-type PRIMPOL but not PRIMPOL∆1–39 was robustly pulled down by CMG, confirming that the PRIMPOL N terminus harbours the primary CMG interaction motifs. PRIMPOL∆1–39 retained primase activity on a ssDNA template (Extended Data Fig. 5b) but was unable to promote fork restart by leading-strand repriming in the human replisome (Fig. 5c,d, lane 4). This defect was not rescued by Pol δ addition (Extended Data Fig. 5c). We conclude that the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG is essential for leading-strand repriming by reconstituted human replisomes.

P values are the result of statistical testing using two-way analysis of cell survival data by fitting a linear quadratic model with maximum likelihood (see Extended Data Table 2 for all P values); pcnaK164R compared with +PRIMPOL∆1–39 P** = 0.0064554, primpol/pcnaK164R compared with +PRIMPOL P* = 0.024598.

According to recent reports, we next investigated whether the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG functions exclusively in PRIMPOL recruitment or whether accurate positioning of the AEP domain is necessary for efficient replication fork restart. Abolishing PRIMPOL interaction with MCM7 by removing the α-helix at the extreme N terminus of PRIMPOL (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL∆1–21) resulted in a modest reduction in leading-strand restart (Fig. 5c, denaturing, lane 5), with a disproportionate effect on initiation events that occurred closest to the CPD (Fig. 5d, Urea PAGE, lane 5). Retaining α-helix 1–21 but substituting the ensuing loop (aa 22–39) with a glycine–serine linker (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOLGS22–39), or substituting six residues in the loop to alanine (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL6A loop), resulted in complete loss of restart products (Fig. 5c,d, lanes 6 and 7). These results highlight the importance of this loop, which sits between MCM4 and the PRIMPOL AEP domain, for leading-strand restart.

Furthermore, targeting three loop residues that sit at the interface with MCM4 (Arg31, Leu32 and Ser33; Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL3A loop) resulted in a less severe defect than a mutant targeting the side chains of Tyr28 and Arg29 to disrupt the bridging interaction between MCM4 and the PRIMPOL AEP domain (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL2A loop) (Fig. 5c–e). This observation strongly suggests that rigid PRIMPOL positioning alongside the MCM C-tier is necessary for efficient leading-strand restart in the human replisome.

In our reconstituted system, the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG (Fig. 5c), but not between PRIMPOL RBMs and RPA (Fig. 3b), is essential for fork restart. Therefore, because PRIMPOL RBM-A is required for PRIMPOL activity in cells9,11,16,17, we hypothesized that the RBM-mediated interaction might serve to increase the local concentration of PRIMPOL at the replication fork. This function may not be required under our standard in vitro reaction conditions, which use a relatively high concentration (20 nM) of PRIMPOL. To test this idea, we performed a titration of wild-type PRIMPOL and PRIMPOLΔRBM. With wild-type PRIMPOL, leading-strand restart became less efficient only when the protein concentration was reduced to 0.1 nM (Fig. 5f and Extended Data Fig. 5d). By contrast, leading-strand restart was compromised at 1 nM PRIMPOLΔRBM and was barely detectable at 0.1 nM. These findings are consistent with a model in which the RBM-mediated interaction between PRIMPOL and RPA facilitates PRIMPOL localization at the replication fork.

It has been revealed that loss of PRIMPOL does not sensitize many human cell lines to DNA damage because of redundant DNA damage tolerance pathways27,28,29. Therefore, to evaluate whether the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG is required for PRIMPOL function in human cells, we took advantage of our recent finding that loss of PRIMPOL sensitizes translesion synthesis (TLS)-deficient TK6 lymphoblastoid cells to cisplatin, most prominently observed in cells unable to ubiquitinate PCNA at lysine 164 (ref. 27). PRIMPOL was removed by CRISPR–Cas9 targeting in pcnaK164R cells. Figure 5g shows that loss of PRIMPOL further sensitized pcnaK164R cells to cisplatin, consistent with our previous work27. Whereas expression of wild-type PRIMPOL fully rescued this phenotype, expression of PRIMPOL∆1–39 did not complement the additional cisplatin sensitivity of pcnaK164R cells (Fig. 5g, Extended Data Fig. 6 and Extended Data Table 2). These data indicate that the interaction between CMG and PRIMPOL, which is essential for fork restart in vitro, is notable for PRIMPOL-mediated DNA damage tolerance in human cells.

On the basis of our results and previous work, we propose the following model for replication fork restart by PRIMPOL-dependent repriming (Fig. 6a). Our biochemical reconstitution has demonstrated that the PRIMPOL RBMs are not essential for leading-strand repriming in vitro. However, they do become crucial for fork restart at low PRIMPOL concentrations, and evidence from cellular studies shows that RBM-A is required for PRIMPOL recruitment to chromatin and fork progression during replication stress9,11,16,17. To accommodate these observations, we propose that the interaction of PRIMPOL with RPA, which is low affinity11 and therefore likely to be transient, serves primarily to localize PRIMPOL to actively replicating genomic loci, which may be necessary because PRIMPOL is a relatively low abundance protein in human cells15,30 (Fig. 6a).

According to recent reports, a, Model for CMG-directed replication fork restart by PRIMPOL after the replisome encounters a leading-strand DNA lesion (red triangle). Two non-mutually exclusive mechanisms are shown. In (i), PRIMPOL is recruited to CMG only after fork stalling at the lesion. In (ii), PRIMPOL can associate with CMG and travel with the replisome before fork stalling. b, Composite model of the human replisome showing the positions of PRIMPOL, Pol ε and Pol α–primase. The model is a composite of the following PDB files: 8B9D, 7PFO and 9F6D. The position of the Pol ε catalytic domain (9F6D) is based on a yeast replisome structure42.

Industry observers note that on encountering a DNA lesion, leading-strand synthesis by Pol ε is blocked, but CMG continues to translocate along the template at a greatly reduced rate1,2, exposing ssDNA on the leading-strand template between the helicase and polymerase (Fig. 6a). Through its interactions with MCM4 and MCM7, PRIMPOL is positioned to capture the exposed ssDNA to initiate leading-strand repriming (Fig. 6a, pathway (i)). After primer synthesis, Pol ε must reengage the leading strand for optimal fork progression to resume. The anchoring of PRIMPOL on CMG suggests a pathway in which the primer might be handed off directly to the leading-strand PCNA loader CTF18-RFC and then to Pol ε. Alternatively, Pol δ might facilitate the recoupling of leading-strand synthesis by extending the primer made by PRIMPOL until it reaches CMG, at which point the 3′ end is transferred to Pol ε. This pathway has been observed following leading-strand lesion bypass by TLS in the yeast replisome31.

Industry observers note that the direct interaction of PRIMPOL with CMG raises the possibility that PRIMPOL could travel with CMG to facilitate its immediate deployment on helicase–polymerase uncoupling (Fig. 6a, pathway (ii)). In this regard, it is noteworthy that PRIMPOL does not clash with any known core replisome protein, including Pol ε (Fig. 6b). However, because the MCM4 and MCM7 ATPase domains undergo conformational changes during CMG translocation that could affect PRIMPOL binding, single-molecule studies will be required to determine if PRIMPOL can stably associate with moving replisomes.

The mechanism of PRIMPOL recruitment via MCM4 and MCM7 ensures that repriming is tightly coupled to CMG progression to limit the size of the ssDNA gap that is left for post-replicative repair pathways. Our work further establishes that PRIMPOL displays a sequence preference for primer synthesis. Based on prior studies, this sequence is short and somewhat degenerate25, which should enable efficient repriming at most genomic loci. However, regions of the genome devoid of optimal priming sites are likely to exist, for example in repetitive DNA, which could limit repriming and bias fork restart and stabilisation towards alternative pathways.

Sources indicate that the two-stage model for PRIMPOL recruitment involving both RPA and CMG interactions is analogous to a mechanism proposed for the recruitment of TLS polymerases to the replication fork32. This mechanism has been observed in the E. coli replisome for the TLS polymerase PolIV, where an interaction with the single-stranded DNA-binding protein SSB concentrates PolIV at the fork to promote its interaction with the sliding clamp β33. We also note that RPA will accumulate on the leading-strand template during prolonged uncoupling, which should enhance PRIMPOL recruitment to stressed replication forks.

Apart from its low abundance, PRIMPOL activity is regulated by checkpoint and cell cycle kinases6,34,35,36, suggesting that excessive repriming and daughter-strand gap formation is deleterious. Tight regulation of PRIMPOL might also indicate a capacity of the enzyme to interfere with normal replisome function. We reasoned that this could be a consequence of PRIMPOL being directed to the leading strand by CMG, causing it to interfere with Pol ε by competing for the nascent leading strand. Consistent with this idea, addition of PRIMPOL mildly slowed fork progression on an undamaged template, and this effect was exacerbated by omission of CTF18-RFC, which compromises PCNA loading on the leading strand (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Importantly, this inhibition was dependent on the interaction of PRIMPOL with CMG but not on primase activity (Extended Data Fig. 7b).

It has been revealed that the widespread phylogenetic distribution of PRIMPOL37, and the conservation of its CMG interaction motifs, indicates an evolutionary pressure to keep replication forks moving by repriming. It also indicates that in the absence of chronic replication stress, repriming might be the default response of the replisome to impediments to leading-strand synthesis. This raises the possibility that leading-strand synthesis might be considerably more discontinuous in human cells than previously appreciated. It is also interesting to consider that PRIMPOL could access the leading strand for priming potentially in any instance where synthesis is paused, for example during PCNA loading on the leading strand by CTF18-RFC. This is possibly a frequent occurrence because PCNA abundance is reported to be similar on leading and lagging strands in yeast38.

Multiple pathways collaborate to protect and restart stalled replication forks during replication stress. Ablating replication fork reversal factors has been found to promote fork progression in a PRIMPOL-dependent manner6,34,39,40,41, suggesting an interplay between repriming and replication fork remodelling. The factors that dictate the balance between repriming and other fork processing pathways (for example, fork reversal), and how this is influenced by the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction, is an notable area for future study, especially given that PRIMPOL promotes chemoresistance in BRCA1 deficient cells34.

It has been revealed that for decades, prokaryotic and eukaryotic replisomes were thought to function with a single primase to initiate DNA synthesis on both template strands. This changed with the discovery of PRIMPOL as a second primase in many eukaryotic species, including humans7,8,9. However, although it has been demonstrated that PRIMPOL facilitates replication fork progression during replication stress in a range of metazoan cell lines, evidence for PRIMPOL primase activity being directed specifically to the leading-strand template, and a plausible mechanism for this targeting, was lacking. The work presented here demonstrates that, through its interactions with CMG, PRIMPOL is a dedicated leading-strand primase, establishing a division of labour in the human replisome: Pol α–primase acts on the lagging strand14, while PRIMPOL operates on the leading strand. Our data, together with the strong conservation of CMG-binding motifs in the PRIMPOL N terminus, indicate that many eukaryotic replisomes rely on strand-specific primases to maintain efficient replisome progression, and that this specificity is governed by helicase-directed primase recruitment to the replication fork.

Sources indicate that replication reactions were performed essentially as described previously, with the following modifications. Reactions were assembled stepwise: DNA (2.4 nM) was first incubated with CMG (50 nM) for 10 min in replication buffer supplemented with 0.1 mM AMP-PNP. Following this pre-incubation, the mixture was diluted two-fold with replication buffer containing 30 μM dATP and dCTP. Additional replication factors (20 nM PCNA, 20 nM RFC, 20 nM Pol ε, 10 nM Pol α, 20 nM CLASPIN, 20 nM TIM–TIPIN, 20 nM AND1 and 20 nM CTF18-RFC) were included at this stage unless stated otherwise. Replication was initiated by adding a concentrated start mix supplying 4 mM ATP; 30 µM dTTP and dGTP; 200 µM GTP, CTP and UTP; 33 nM α-[32P]-dCTP; and 100 nM RPA. When present, 20 nM PRIMPOL was added 2–3 min after replication had started. For reactions containing Pol δ, potassium glutamate was increased to 250 mM, and the polymerase was added at 2 nM immediately before the start mix. Leading-strand restart reactions were typically incubated for 20–40 min and terminated with EDTA to 50 mM. Unincorporated radiolabel was removed using Illustra MicroSpin G-50 columns. Replication products were separated by alkaline agarose electrophoresis (0.7% agarose, 30 mM NaOH, 2 mM EDTA) run for 16.5 h at 24 V, fixed in cold 5% trichloroacetic acid, dried on Whatman paper, and visualized using an Amersham Typhoon phosphorimager scanner.

It has been revealed that for analysis under native conditions, terminated reactions were supplemented with SDS (0.1%) and proteinase K (0.2 mg ml−1; New England Biolabs) and incubated for 10 min at 37 °C. DNA was purified by phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol extraction (25:24:1; TE-equilibrated) and passed through Illustra MicroSpin G-50 columns to remove unincorporated nucleotides. Samples were then digested with SapI–PciI for 30 min at 37 °C to remove the template ends and prevent end-labelled species in gels. Following digestion, reactions underwent a second SDS/proteinase K treatment and phenol:chloroform extraction to ensure complete protein removal. DNA was ethanol-precipitated, washed with 70% ethanol, resuspended in native loading dye (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 50 mM EDTA, 10% Ficoll 400, 2% N-lauroylsarcosine sodium salt solution), and resolved on 1% agarose gels run overnight at 24 V in modified 1× TAE buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.9, 40 mM sodium acetate, 1 mM EDTA pH 8.0). Gels were dried and imaged as described above.

In a recent development, for two-dimensional (2D) gel analysis, samples were prepared as for native conditions and loaded into two lanes of a native agarose gel, with 10% of the reaction applied to one lane and the remaining 90% to the other. After electrophoresis, the lane containing the bulk of the sample was excised and placed horizontally along the top of a 0.7% denaturing agarose gel for the second dimension, which was run for 16.5 h at 27 V. Gels were then processed and imaged as described for alkaline gels.

For analysis on denaturing polyacrylamide gels, samples were prepared as for native conditions, but digested with SalI–NruI instead, and resuspended in loading dye (95% formamide, 20 mM EDTA, 0.04% Bromophenol Blue and 0.04% xylene cyanol). Samples were boiled for 5 min at 75 °C and resolved on a 40 cm × 20 cm 3.5% denaturing polyacrylamide gel. Gels were run in 1× TBE for 150 min at 40 W and dried as described above.

DNA substrates were prepared following previously published methods1,20. Gapped pZN3 was produced by introducing two adjacent Nt.BbvCI nicks and heating the plasmid to release the short intervening oligonucleotide, which was subsequently displaced using a sequestering oligonucleotide. The resulting gapped plasmid was purified on a Sepharose 4B (Sigma-Aldrich 4B200) gel filtration column. A 10-fold molar excess of a short oligonucleotide containing a CPD lesion, an abasic site or an undamaged control sequence (listed in Supplementary Table 1) was then annealed into the gap and ligated to generate the damaged or control templates. Finally, the DNA was digested with SapI, ligated to a pre-annealed fork structure, and purified again over a Sepharose 4B column.

Sources indicate that replication proteins were expressed in either E. coli or insect cells (Sf9 and Hi-5) and were purified following the methods described previously20,43. For more details about the purification steps, see Supplementary Table 2.

Industry observers note that relevant plasmids for protein expression were transformed into Rosetta2 cells using standard bacterial transformation protocols. A single transformant colony was selected and cultured in 1 l LB media supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin and 10 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol overnight at 30 °C without agitation. The following morning, the culture temperature was increased to 37 °C and incubated with shaking at 210 rpm. On reaching an optical density (OD600) of 0.6–0.8, protein expression was induced by the addition of 1 mM IPTG for 3 h. Cells were subsequently harvested, washed with PBS and flash-frozen for storage.

It has been revealed that wild-type and mutant PRIMPOL proteins were purified using the following protocol. Cell pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 1 M NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.1% Triton X-100, 0.5 mM TCEP and protease inhibitors (cOmplete, EDTA-free; Roche). The cells were lysed by sonication (three cycles of 1 min each, consisting of 5 s ‘on’ and 5 s ‘off’ pulses at 40% amplitude), and insoluble material was removed by centrifugation at 235,000g for 50 min at 4 °C. The clarified lysate was incubated with 1 ml Strep-Tactin XT Superflow high-capacity resin for 1 h at 4 °C. The resin was then collected and washed extensively with 100 ml lysis buffer, followed by sequential washes with 25 ml lysis buffer containing 0.55 M NaCl and 35 ml lysis buffer containing 0.1 M NaCl to reduce the salt concentration. Bound protein was eluted in 1 ml fractions using eight column volumes of 0.1 M NaCl lysis buffer supplemented with 30 mM biotin. Protein-containing fractions were pooled and loaded onto a 5 ml HiTrap Heparin HP column pre-equilibrated in 0.1 M NaCl buffer. The protein was eluted with a 20 column volume linear gradient from 100 mM to 1 M NaCl. Peak fractions were pooled and dialysed overnight against 1 l of storage buffer containing 25 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.6), 0.3 M potassium acetate, 10% glycerol, 0.02% NP-40-S and 0.5 mM TCEP. Finally, the protein was concentrated using a 30 kDa molecular weight cut-off spin concentrator (Amicon Ultra-30), flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C.

In a recent development, reactions (20 µl) were performed in buffer containing 25 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.6, 150 mM potassium glutamate, 10 mM magnesium acetate, 0.05% NP-40, and 1 mM DTT. A 2 µl aliquot was removed as input, and the remaining mixture was incubated with 5 µl α-Flag magnetic beads equilibrated in buffer for 30 min at 4 °C with shaking (1,250 rpm). Beads were washed three times with 100 µl reaction buffer, and bound proteins were eluted for 30 min at 4 °C at 1,250 rpm in 20 µl buffer containing 0.2 mg ml−1 Flag peptide. Eluates were mixed with loading buffer and analysed by 4–12% SDS–PAGE alongside input samples, followed by silver staining and western blotting.

PRIMPOL, purified as described above, was concentrated using an Amicon Ultra centrifugal filter with a 30 kDa MWCO and injected onto a 2.4 ml S200 increase 3.2/300 column equilibrated with 40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.6, 80 mM KOAc, 1 mM DTT. The peak fractions were collected and adjusted with buffer to a concentration of 5.7 µM. CMG was dialysed overnight against 40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.6, 80 mM KOAc, 1 mM DTT, mixed with 1.3-fold molar excess of PRIMPOL, supplemented with 3.3 mM ATP and incubated on ice for at least 20 min before cryo-EM grid preparation. After incubation on ice, 2 µl of the sample was applied to freshly glow-discharged (Edwards Sputter Coater S150B, 45 s at 30 mA) UltrAuFoil R1.2/1.3, manually blotted on the top face for 2 s and immediately plunged into liquid ethane at liquid nitrogen temperature. Two datasets of 8,160 and 8,103 raw movies, respectively, were acquired using a 300 kV TFS Titan Krios microscope equipped with a Falcon 4i direct electron detector operated in electron counting mode using ThermoFisher EPU with AFIS enabled. The movies were collected over a defocus range of −1.0 µm to −2.6 µm, at an effective pixel size of 0.84 Å per pixel.

Recent findings suggest that the data processing pipeline is shown as a schematic in Extended Data Fig. 4a. Raw movies were motion-corrected and dose-weighted using the implementation of a MotionCor2-like program of RELION44,45 (Extended Data Table 1) and then imported to CryoSPARC v.4.7.1 (ref. 46) for further processing. For each dataset, the particles were first ‘blob’-picked and extracted with 4-fold binning (336 Å box size). The 2D classification was run on a subset of 50,000 particles, and classes showing features for CMG in 2D-class averages were selected. Ab initio reconstruction was performed with the selected particles and, separately, with the remaining particles to generate three-dimensional (3D) volumes for either CMG or ‘noise/junk’-classes. The obtained volumes were provided as 3D references in two iterative rounds of heterogeneous refinement of all extracted particles, the first round of which the particles of the best class were selected for the second round. Independently, 2D class averages were used for template-based picking, and the resulting particles were also subjected to two iterative rounds of heterogeneous refinement as described above. The particles of the best 3D class from each picking strategy were combined and duplicate particles were removed. The resulting particles were used for homogeneous refinement with minimization over per-particle scale enabled, after which the particle population with poor signal (relative per-particle scale below 0.75) was removed. The remaining particles were subjected to 3D classification using a focus mask around the C-tier of the MCM ring, and particle classes with good definition for secondary structure features in the MCM C-tier were selected. At this stage, particles from datasets 1 and 2 were combined and locally refined using a focus mask around the AAA+ ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7. The resulting 3D reconstruction displayed density for the AEP domain of PRIMPOL around which a local mask was drawn for 3D classification. The largest class (135,661 particles) also exhibited the strongest signal for PRIMPOL. The particles were recentred on a mask around PRIMPOL and ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7, re-extracted (280-pixel box, downsampled to 160 pixels, 1.47 Å per pixel) and subjected to signal subtraction with an inverted mask around PRIMPOL and ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7. The subtracted particles were used for 3D classification from which the classes with the best density for the PRIMPOL AEP domain were selected (65,500 particles). The 30,000-particle subset with the best per-particle scale was then used for 3DFlex47 to reconstruct the final map for the PRIMPOL AEP domain near the AAA+ ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7 (map 1, 3.5 Å resolution). The same particle subset was reverted to the original (non-subtracted) images, re-extracted from the original micrographs without binning (440-pixel box, 0.84 Å per pixel) using particle poses from global refinement on the CMG helicase. The obtained particles were subjected to homogeneous refinement to reconstruct a consensus map (map 2), or to local refinements with either a focus mask on CMG components GINS, CDC45 and the N-tier of the MCM ring (map 3, 3.1 Å resolution), or a focus mask on the C-tier of the MCM ring (map 4, 3.3 Å resolution). Maps coloured by estimated local resolution are shown in Extended Data Fig. 4c. Fourier shell correlation plots are shown in Extended Data Fig. 4d. Focus maps (maps 1, 3 and 4) were fitted into the consensus volume (map 2) using ChimeraX48. An initial atomic model was obtained by rigid-body fitting previously reported structures of CMG (6XTX, 7PFO) and PRIMPOL (5L2X) into the consensus EM volume using ChimeraX26,43,49. The fit-to-density was subsequently refined using ISOLDE50 inside ChimeraX. ATP–ADP ligands and gaps in the model were built de novo in Coot51. The molecular model was then used together with the consensus map and all focus maps to generate a composite EM map using phenix.combine_focused_maps by Thomas Terwilliger. Model geometry and atomic displacement parameters were refined against the composite map using phenix.real_space_refine52, after which model validation was carried out using MolProbity53 inside Phenix. Statistics for cryo-EM data acquisition, processing and molecular model refinement are summarized in Extended Data Table 1. Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between PRIMPOL–CMG (this study) and PRIMPOL–DNA (5L2X) was calculated in PyMOL (www.pymol.org) for 1,987 pairs of common atoms (RMSD = 1.723) or 253 pairs of common Cα atoms (RMSD = 1.374).

Sources indicate that all TK6 cell lines were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium with GlutaMAX (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco). The cells were grown at 37 °C and 5% CO2. The cells were maintained between 0.05 cells ml −1 and 1.0 × 106 cells ml−1.

For the generation of plasmids for protein purification, plasmid MT_FB (see Supplementary Table 4 for details) was used as a template to generate the rest of PRIMPOL mutants in this study.

Recent findings suggest that for the generation of plasmids for cellular studies, the m6p-PRIMPOL-WT_GFP_BSD plasmid backbone (wild-type PRIMPOL with GFP tag) (Supplementary Table 4) was used to generate the PRIMPOL ∆1–39 mutant (truncation mutant with GFP co-expression), using the Q5 Site-Directed Mutagenesis Kit (NEB) as per kit instructions. See Supplementary Table 1 for primers used.

TK6 primpol/pcnaK164R cells were used for expression of mutant and wild-type PRIMPOL–GFP. PRIMPOL Δ1–39 and wild-type PRIMPOL were expressed through plasmids that contained resistance cassettes for blasticidin. Plasmid DNA (15 µg) was electroporated into 20 × 106 cells using the Neon electroporator (Thermo Fisher) with the following conditions: 100 µl Resuspension Buffer R, 1,400 V and 20 ms. The electroporated cells were seeded across 96-well plates in growth media containing 7.5 µg ml−1 blasticidin. The surviving colonies were expanded and subjected to single-cell sorting for positive GFP expression through FACS to generate clonal populations.

According to recent reports, viscous culture medium (5 ml) consisting of 11.9 g l−1 RPMI 1640 powder with l-glutamine supplement (Gibco), 2 g l−1 sodium hydrogen carbonate (Sigma-Aldrich), 10 g l−1 4,000 cP methylcellulose (Thermo Fisher), 100 U l−1 penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco) and 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco) was added to wells of six-well plates. The plates were equilibrated at 37 °C, 10% CO2 for a minimum of 1 h. The cells were treated with the indicated dose of cisplatin for 1 h at 37 °C and 10% CO2. The cells were then pelleted at 1,200 rpm for 5 min and resuspended in fresh growth media to stop the cisplatin treatment. Then, 500,000, 50,000 or 5,000 cells were added to duplicate wells of the six-well plates for each cell line or condition. The plates were incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO2 until well-defined colonies were visible.

Flow cytometry was used to confirm the expression of GFP in TK6 primpol/pcnaK164R cell lines. A total of 1 × 106 cells were pelleted at 1,200 rpm for 5 min and resuspended in 1 ml PBS supplemented with 2% FBS. The cells were analysed by flow cytometry using a Becton Dickinson LSRFortessa. TK6 primpol and TK6 wild-type cells were used as negative controls for GFP expression. Cell sorting of GFP-positive cells was performed using a Becton Dickinson FACSAria Fusion, with cells sorted into single cells per well of a 96-well plate. Flow cytometry data were plotted using FlowJo.

Industry observers note that for the colony survival assay in TK6 human cells in Fig. 5g, individual colonies in each well were counted using a custom macro-script in ImageJ, and the percentage survival relative to untreated cells was calculated to assess clonogenic survival. Statistical testing was performed by the R package CFAssay using two-way analysis of the cell survival data by fitting a linear quadratic model with maximum likelihood (Extended Data Table 2).

Statistics for cryo-EM data acquisition, processing and molecular model refinement are summarized in Extended Data Table 1. DNA replication assays were quantified using ImageJ, and data were plotted in Prism.

Experiments in Figs. 1c, 3d and 5b and Extended Data Figs. 1a,c–e, 2b, 3b, 5c and 7a,b were performed twice. Colony survival assay in TK6 human cells (Fig. 5g) was performed three times, testing two independent clones of primpol/pcnaK164R + PRIMPOLΔ1–39. Cryo-EM sample preparation was performed twice.

In the latest episode of AC Milan’s The Chamber series, Mario Gila was the guest and spoke about the positive mental health journey that he’s at the moment on.

It was last month that Milan unveiled their new series, called The Chamber, which focuses on the mental health of the players at the club. Luka Modric was the first guest, a perfect start in many ways, and the second episode has now been published with Mario Gila as the guest.
